meta.what: Grade the whole low-confidence pool with the calibrated Claude grader, and pick what both passes call a story.

spans.summary: The Gemara cites an incident where a woman died and her fetus was observed moving three times after her death to challenge a medical assumption.
The ministering angels ask God why Israel does not recite Hallel on Rosh HaShana, and God responds that it is inappropriate while the books of life and death are open.
During the destruction of the First Temple, the Levites remained on their platform singing a specific psalm until the enemies arrived and conquered them.
When Rava falls ill, Abaye and other Sages visit him and engage in a legal debate regarding the opinion of the Rabbis in a baraita about valuations.
Rav Hisda recalls receiving physical blows from his teacher Avimi as a result of his questioning a specific legal tradition regarding the proclamation of orphans' property.
Mareimar collects a marriage contract from the property of orphans, leading to a debate between Ravina and Ameimar regarding the legal justification for such an act.
Rav Naḥman describes how he initially refused to collect debts from orphans until he heard a teaching from Rav Huna that changed his judicial practice.
A man sells his land and then divorces his wife, leading her to sue the buyers for her marriage contract payment, prompting a legal inquiry from Rav Yosef to Rav Pappa.
A man who sold his property appeared before Rav Yeimar, who instructed the court to remove the man's phylacteries as part of the assets to be handed over.
A man in Pumbedita dedicated his property and sought Rav Yehuda's guidance, who instructed him to desacralize it using four dinars and throwing them into the river.
Moses rebukes the Jewish people for being ingrates because they did not ask God to grant them the faithful heart He wished for them at Sinai.
Rav Yosef physically turns his face away to show his displeasure with Rav Huna for stating what he considered a redundant legal ruling.
A dispute arises over a promissory note with an unusual date, leading Rav Aha bar Yaakov to investigate the scribal dating customs of the time.
Antoninus habitually smuggles gold to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi inside sacks of wheat to hide the wealth from his servants.
Antoninus shows extreme humility by personally serving Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and offering himself as a footstool for the Rabbi to climb into bed.
Upon the deaths of Antoninus and the Persian king Adrakan, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rav respectively lament the end of their unique relationships with these rulers.
Upon the death of Rabban Gamliel the Elder, Onkelos the convert burned a vast sum of Tyrian coinage to honor him.
An incident occurred where a man swallowed a water leech, and Rabbi Neḥunya permitted heating water for him on Shabbat to save his life.
Rabbi Ya’akov and Rabbi Yirmeya purchase goods at a pagan fair and subsequently rebuke each other for acting against the perceived standards of their teachers.
Rav Hisda tells Avimei that Abraham's version of the tractate was much larger than theirs, leading into a discussion of a specific difficulty in the current Mishna.
Rav Huna sells a cow to a gentile and justifies his action to Rav Hisda by claiming the buyer intended to slaughter it.
Rabba sells a donkey to a Jew suspected of illicit trade, and Abaye challenges him on the propriety of the sale.
The household of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi paid a massive bribe to delay delivering a fattened ox to the Roman authorities until after their festival day.
Rabbi Zeira travels between different academies in Babylonia and Eretz Yisrael, eventually identifying the correct attributions for a legal tradition regarding animal slaughter.
A woman confesses her grave sins to Rav Hisda and subsequently dies, serving as a case study for the fate of those who repent from heresy or severe sin.
Levi and Rabbi Shimon finish a book of study and disagree on which book to learn next, leading Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to teach that one should learn what their heart desires.
Rav Hisda warns his students that one should learn from multiple teachers, and upon hearing this, they immediately leave him to seek other instructors.
Rav Geviha provides an alternative version of the incident involving Rava and a partnership with a gentile regarding orla saplings.
A gentile midwife responds to an insult by boasting that she secretly kills the Jewish babies she delivers.
Abaye recounts how he was unable to find a cure for his ailment until an Arab provided a remedy involving burnt olive seeds, which successfully healed him.
The text begins to describe an ailment suffered by Rabbi Ya'akov.
Rabbi Abbahu suffers from an earache and receives medical instructions from Rabbi Yoḥanan or the Sages.
Several Amoraim attempt to prepare and consume a specific medicinal remedy using different physical techniques.
While sitting with Shmuel, the gentile scholar Ablet pulls his hand away from cooked wine to avoid making it forbidden, but Shmuel tells him it is permitted.
An attendant who fell asleep next to an uncovered jug of water asks Rav Ḥilkiya bar Tovi if his presence prevented a snake from drinking from it.
Rabbi Yoḥanan travels to Parod and asks for the teachings of the late Bar Kappara, leading Rabbi Tanḥum to recite a ruling which Yoḥanan then praises using a biblical metaphor.
Rav Shmuel bar Bisna visits Marguan and refuses both wine and beer offered to him, leading the Gemara to analyze his reasons.
Ravina permits Rav Hiyya to use a certain vessel for beer, and Rav Hiyya proceeds to do so.
Rabbi Akiva visits Ginzak and is unable to answer the residents' legal questions, so he returns to the study hall to seek the rulings from the Sages.
Aivu is seen eating gentile bread at the edge of fields, leading Rava to instruct his students to stop speaking with him.
When Rav dismisses Rabbi Simlai's testimony by insulting his town, Shmuel offers to summon the rabbi, causing Rav to become embarrassed.

Rabbi Zeira recounts a chain of sages who struggled to find a ruling until Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, upon hearing Rabbi Ḥiyya's tradition, ordered his own previous teachings to be discarded in favor of it.
Yosei ben Yo’ezer physically marked domain boundaries with stakes to clarify impurity laws, and later people consulted Rabbi Yannai regarding a related case.
Rabbi Ḥiyya of Parva visits the Exilarch and is asked by the attendants for a ruling on eggs roasted by gentiles.
Rabbi Abbahu reports an incident of an old man in his neighborhood who would smooth the surface of salkondarit salt with fat, providing a reason for its prohibition.
Shmuel's father and Levi would enter and pray in the Shaf VeYativ synagogue in Nehardea despite the presence of a royal statue.
Rav Sheshet, who was blind, was being led by his attendant and instructed him to make him run when they reached a certain idolatrous tree.
Rav Amram consults Rav Yosef regarding a garden fertilized with idol-worship dung, and Rav Yosef rules it permitted based on Shmuel's tradition.
A man whose wine was mixed with forbidden libation wine seeks guidance from Rav Hisda, who instructs him to dispose of the value of the forbidden wine to permit the rest.
Rav Yosef bar Abba reports that Rabba bar Yirmeya came to his town and cited a baraita regarding stones of Mercury.
When Ulla arrived in Babylonia, he sat on a damaged idolatrous platform, prompting a legal debate with Rav Yehuda over whether such an object remains prohibited.
A baraita records philosophers asking the Sages in Rome why God does not eliminate idolatry.
A six-year-old child who had mastered the laws of idolatry is consulted by people on the legality of treading grapes with a gentile, and he provides a reasoned ruling.
Rabbi Yirmeya visits Savta and prohibits the local Jews from drinking wine that had been diluted by gentiles.
A gentile stops a wine leak by placing his hand over the hole, leading Rav Pappa to rule that only the wine directly adjacent to the hand is prohibited.
The household of Parzak the vizier stored wine with their gentile sharecroppers, and Rava ruled it prohibited because the sharecroppers' fear of the vizier would lead them to cover up any tampering.
Certain gentiles came to Rabba bar Avuh to convert, and he instructed them to sell their idolatrous property before finalizing their conversion so they could keep the proceeds.
Rav Hillel reports an incident where a mouse fell into vinegar in Rav Kahana's study hall and Rav Kahana ruled it forbidden.
A gentile girl is found holding wine froth near barrels, and Rava rules the wine permitted because she likely took the froth from the outside.
An army enters Neharde'a and opens wine barrels, and Rabbi Elazar subsequently permits the wine.
A wine shop owner gives her key to a gentile woman, and the Sages rule the wine is permitted as she only entrusted her with the key's safekeeping.
A man promises to sell land to one person but sells it to another, leading Rav Yosef to rule that the first buyer's acquisition stands.
A man agrees to sell land for 100 dinars but sells it to another for 120, resulting in Rav Kahana ruling in favor of the first buyer.
Rabba bar Rav Huna visited the house of the Exilarch and drank from a multi-tubed vessel.
A man asks Rabbi Hiyya for someone to purify his newly purchased winepress, and Rabbi Hiyya sends Rav with instructions to act carefully.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef buys an earthen vessel and intends to immerse it until Rabbi Ya’akov informs him of Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling that only metal requires immersion.
Mar bar Rav Ashi recalls an incident where his father received a silver goblet as collateral from a gentile, immersed it, and used it.
Marimar and Mar Zutra would demolish and rebuild their seasonal homes during the opposite seasons to ensure they always had a place to stay.
When Ronya buys land next to Ravina, Ravina considers evicting him, but Rav Safra convinces him to let the poor man stay.
Two brothers divide their father's estate, and the one who received the garden builds a wall that blocks the light of the one who received the hall.
A case involving orphans with a promissory note and a borrower with a receipt is brought before Rav Hama, who rules that the debt cannot be collected but the note should not be destroyed.
The mother of King Shapur sends money to Rav Yosef for a 'great mitzva,' prompting him to determine what that mitzva is.
Rabbi (Judah HaNasi) once appointed two brothers to be in charge of the charity fund.
Rava forced Rav Natan bar Ami to contribute four hundred zuz to charity.
Rabba initially refused to sit on synagogue mats bought with charity funds until he learned that the townspeople have the right to change the designation of such funds.
A poor person approaches Rav Pappa for charity and is ignored, leading Rav Sama to rebuke Rav Pappa for his inaction.
Rav Pappa nearly falls from a ladder and concludes that this near-accident was a divine punishment for failing to properly assist a poor person.
A man who bought land adjacent to his father's estate requests that specific plot upon his father's death, leading to a dispute with his brothers and a ruling by Rav Yosef.
Rabbi Yehuda cites an incident where Baitos ben Zunin owned a combined scroll of eight Prophets with the approval of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
The Sages tell Rav Hamnuna that Rabbi Ami wrote four hundred Torah scrolls, and Rav Hamnuna skeptically suggests he only wrote a single verse four hundred times.
A sage sitting before Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani claims that Job was merely a parable and never actually existed, prompting a rebuttal from the Rabbi.
While Ravina and Rav Hama debated the repentance of Ishmael, Rava dozed off, only to wake up and provide the definitive answer.
The Gemara recounts the historical evolution of the Jewish school system, culminating in Yehoshua ben Gamla's decree to establish local schools to prevent the loss of Torah knowledge.
It contains a specific incident where Rava grants a legal exemption to Rabbi Yoshiya and Rav Ovadya, though it is embedded within a larger legal discussion.
Basket sellers bring goods to Babylonia, are blocked by locals, and Ravina rules on their right to sell to other outsiders.
Wool sellers in Pum Nahara are blocked by locals and Rav Kahana rules on the conditions under which they may sell.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks a pedantic question about a chick's legs and is subsequently expelled from the study hall.
Ravina permits a barrel of wine found in a vineyard of forbidden orla grapes, reasoning that thieves would not hide stolen goods in the same place they stole them.
Rava permits wine found in jugs between vines, assuming it does not belong to a gentile.
Rav Sheshet, who was blind, instructs his servant to position him for prayer in any direction except east, explaining his reasoning.
The household of bar Maryon caused harm to neighbors while beating flax, leading the neighbors to bring the case before Ravina.
A man sells all his 'bar Sisin' property but later claims a specific parcel known by that name was not included in the sale.
A property owner challenges a possessor, who claims he bought it, but the owner argues he was away in the outer markets and thus could not protest.

A man challenges a land possessor who claims to have bought the field from a third party who supposedly bought it from the original owner. A claimant successfully argues that a possessor has no standing because the possessor admits the land wasn't bought from the claimant, leading Rava to rule in the claimant's favor.
A guarantor and debtor dispute whether a repaid debt was subsequently re-borrowed, leading Rav Idi bar Avin to seek a ruling from Abaye.
It introduces a new legal dispute with different claims and evidence, though the narrative outcome and the rabbi's ruling follow in the subsequent text.
A man claims to have bought land but can only prove two years of possession, leading Rav Nachman to order the return of the land and its produce.
A man claims to have purchased land and brings a single witness to three years of possession, sparking a debate about the validity of a single witness in such cases.
A man who mortgaged his orchard is threatened by the creditor that unless he sells the land, the creditor will hide the mortgage and claim ownership through three years of possession.
Rav Ḥisda rules in a case according to Rabbi Elazar, prompting the grandsons of Rav to confront him for ignoring their grandfather's authority.
Rava removed a pair of scissors and a book from orphans' possession after a claimant identified them as his own.
Rav acquired a garden for his academy by drawing an image on its wall, demonstrating his legal ruling on acquisition.
When a witness on a document died, his brother and another person came to ratify the signature, leading Ravina and Rav Ashi to debate if such testimony is valid.
Rabbi Oshaya disagrees with his father Rabbi Hama on a ruling and consults his grandfather Rabbi Bisa, leading Rami bar Hama to praise the three generations of scholars.
A man brought a case to Rabbi Ammi, who sent him to Rabbi Abba bar Memel.
A man who opened windows into a shared courtyard sought legal validation from Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei and subsequently from Rabbi Ḥiyya.
A man offered to sell land called 'the house of Hiyya,' and Rav Ashi ruled that since there were two such plots, the seller only intended to sell one.
Abaye challenges Rabba's ruling and assumes Rabba's silence means agreement, only to later discover deeds from Rabba's house that prove Rabba held his original position.
A man sold an olive press 'and its accompaniments,' leading to a dispute over external stores that was brought before Rav Yosef for a ruling.

A man instructs that a house containing 100 barrels be given as a gift, but when it is found to contain 120, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi debate whether the recipient receives the whole house or only the specified capacity.
Rabbi Yohanan and Rav Safra describe sightings of fantastic sea creatures while traveling by ship.
Upon arriving in Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Elazar asks Ze'eiri to identify the scholar who holds Rav's traditions on measures, and Ze'eiri points out Rav Yitzḥak bar Avdimi.
The Gemara contrasts the market practices of Shmuel and his father and reports a message from Eretz Yisrael regarding whose merit is greater.
During a drought, Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina instructs his attendant Puga to store produce for the coming years.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Elazar recall specific physical manifestations of the extreme abundance and famine they witnessed in their youth.
Rabbi Ḥanina travels to rural villages to teach and addresses a contradiction between biblical verses regarding the dimensions of the Sanctuary.
When litigants came before Rav Yitzḥak bar Ami regarding a path through a vineyard, he ruled that the path must be wide enough for a person to carry a load of branches and turn around.

Jonathan, a descendant of Moses, justifies his service as an idolatrous priest through a misunderstood family tradition until King David redirects his love for money by appointing him as the Temple treasurer.
Rav Nittai and Rabbi Tabla attempt to rule according to Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav but are sharply rebuked and stopped by Shmuel.
Rav Huna bar Hiyya intends to rule like Rabbi Zekharya but is challenged by Rav Nahman.
Rabbi Yoḥanan, having lost ten sons, would carry a bone of his tenth son to console others in their grief.
A firstborn sold his deceased brother's portion of an estate, leading the brother's orphans to physically reclaim the produce from the buyers until Rava ruled on the sale's validity.
Mar Zutra, a firstborn, divided a basket of peppers equally with his brothers, and Rav Ashi ruled that this act constituted a waiver of his firstborn rights for the entire estate.
A man proves someone is a firstborn to Rabbi Hanina by testifying that the father used to send people with eye ailments to the son, whose saliva had healing properties unique to a father's firstborn.
After Rav Pappa challenges him with a tradition from Eretz Yisrael, Rava publicly retracts his previous legal ruling, declaring it a mistake.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi initially dismisses a challenge from Rabbi Natan regarding a Mishnaic text but later retracts his answer, admitting his previous response was born of immaturity.

A dying man divides his estate between his daughters and wife, leading Rav Nahman to visit Rav Hisda in Sura to determine if the wife's specific portion of produce causes her to lose her marriage contract rights.
A man divides his property among his wife and two daughters, but after one daughter dies, Rav Pappi must determine how the returned portion affects the wife's share.
Rav Ilish proposes a compromise in a complex inheritance case but is corrected and embarrassed by Rava, who then comforts him with a biblical verse.
When Yonatan ben Uzziel studied Torah, the intensity of his sanctity was so great that any bird flying over him would be burned.
Rav Yosef, having lost his memory due to illness, realizes a logical flaw in a tradition he cited and corrects himself.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef brings a ruling from Eretz Yisrael that contradicts Rav Yosef, prompting Rav Sheshet to dismissively wave his hand.
A dying man declares his wife fit for a High Priest to exempt her from levirate marriage, leading to a debate between Rava and Abaye and a final ruling to remain concerned about her status.
A man declares on his deathbed that he has no brothers, and despite Rav Yosef's argument for leniency, Rava rules that the court must remain concerned about the wife's status.
Rav Huna and Rav Naḥman visit the ailing Rabba bar Avuh and use the opportunity to clarify a halakhic ruling regarding Rabbi Yosei's opinion.
The Gemara cites an incident where a fetus moved three times after its mother had already died to challenge a legal assumption about the order of death.
Shmuel instructs Rav Hana to assemble ten men so he can publicly declare that a fetus can acquire property.
The Gemara cites precedents in Neharde'a and Tiberias where Shmuel and Rabbi Yoḥanan actively intervened to ensure an individual received half of a shared gift.
A man sends silk to his family without instructions, and Rabbi Ami determines the distribution based on which garments are suitable for sons versus daughters.
Rav Pappa transfers twelve thousand zuz located in Bei Huza'ei to Rav Shmuel bar Aḥa by granting him a small piece of land to facilitate the acquisition of the movable property.
After Rav Naḥman responds to a legal question with a silent hand gesture and leaves, Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak asks Rava to interpret the meaning of that physical act.
The Gemara discusses a specific deed that lacked the standard formula regarding the giver's death.
A person sold his father's property during his transition year to adulthood, and Rava ruled the sale void.
Rami bar Hama cites an incident where a specific tied document was brought before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to challenge Rav Huna's definition of where witnesses sign.
A tied document is brought before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who misidentifies the date until Zunin explains the local dating custom, which the Rabbi then adopts.
It features a new actor (Rabbi Hanina) and a distinct legal case involving a different dating convention (Archon), though it follows the common 'case-and-ruling' pattern which can be borderline.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi nearly invalidates a tied document for lacking a date until his son Shimon suggests it is hidden in the folds, which is confirmed upon opening it.
After being expelled from the study hall, Rabbi Yirmeya provides such insightful answers to legal queries sent by his colleagues that he is brought back into the academy.
A dispute arises over a document stating a debt of 'six hundred and a dinar' without specifying the currency, leading Rav Sherevya to consult Abaye.
A woman claims she is not the one who signed a receipt witnessed by Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, and he confirms he does not recognize her.
A promissory note with an anonymous creditor ('from you') is brought before Rav Huna's court, sparking a debate on its validity.
A guarantor who repaid a gentile creditor before the orphans were claimed seeks reimbursement, leading to a legal debate between Rav Mordekhai and Rav Ashi.
Judges in Neharde’a and Pumbedita collected slaves from orphans to pay debts, but Rav Naḥman ordered them to return the property.
Rabba bar bar Hana describes his habit of following Rabbi Yohanan to ask questions and how the Rabbi would only answer after performing his post-lavatory rituals.
Rabbi Abbahu misinterprets Rabbi Yohanan's silence as agreement with his legal conclusion, leading him to cite it in Yohanan's name.
Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sends a legal query to Rav Huna, but Rav Huna passes away before answering, leading his son Rabba to provide the ruling in his stead.
A man built a mansion on land belonging to orphans, and Rav Nahman confiscated the building from him.
Rav Yosef asks Abaye to warn the Tarbu family about their damaging goats, but Abaye refuses, arguing that the burden of fencing lies with the victim.
The Gemara cites two incidents in Neharde’a and Pumbedita where pedestrians broke jugs and were held liable by Shmuel and Rava.
Rav Huna and Rav Adda bar Ahava penalized people who left barley in the public domain by declaring their property ownerless.
Rav Huna declared a group's barley ownerless after they were warned to remove it from the public domain and refused to comply.
Rava slaps Rav Shimi's sandal as a gesture of disparagement while refuting his legal explanation regarding the administration of lashes.
Rabbi Abbahu recites a baraita before Rabbi Yoḥanan, who rejects the teaching and tells him to go teach it outside the study hall.
An ox belonging to Rav Pappa had a toothache, broke into a vessel of beer, drank it, and was healed.
Rava praises Rav Aha bar Ya'akov to Rav Nahman, but when they meet, Rav Aha's questions are so difficult that Rav Nahman asks him to stop.
Despite Neḥunya's dedication to providing water for the public, his own son died of thirst, illustrating God's strictness with the righteous.

An ox falls into a shallow channel and the owner slaughters it immediately out of fear it will die, but Rav Nachman rules the meat forbidden because the owner did not wait to see if it would survive the impact.
Rabbi Ḥanina ben Agil, unable to get an answer from Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba regarding the Ten Commandments, travels to Rabbi Tanḥum who provides a tradition on the matter.
A man cut down another's date palm and was brought before the Exilarch, who ordered him to pay one hundred zuz based on his own knowledge of the tree's value.
Upon hearing that the righteous are the first to perish in a plague, Rav Yosef weeps, and Abaye comforts him by explaining it is a kindness to spare them from seeing the coming evil.
Rav Ami and Rav Asi pull Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa in different directions regarding his teaching, leading him to compare himself to a man with two wives who pluck out all his hair.
A man kicks another's safe into a river, leading the owner to claim it contained a pearl, which Rav Ashi then deliberates upon without reaching a final decision.
Rava questions Rav Naḥman about a thief's liability for a shared animal, leading Rav Naḥman to rule one way in the evening and retract his position the following morning.
Rabbi Yishmael recounts how his family's wealth in the Galilee was lost because they grazed animals improperly and judged cases individually.
An unmarried woman impulsively swears to marry anyone who will discipline her son, but the Sages intervene to dissolve the oath when unworthy men try to hold her to it.
While walking with Rav Yehuda, Shmuel veers off the main road to avoid obstacles, demonstrating the practical application of Joshua's stipulations.

While walking, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya observe Rabbi Yehuda ben Kanosa refusing to veer off the road; Rabbi Hiyya explains his student's pious motivations, leading to a respectful encounter.
The prophets instituted the regular Monday and Thursday Torah readings after the Israelites became exhausted from traveling three days in the desert without the 'water' of Torah.
An ox injures a child's hand, and when Rava orders an appraisal, the court officers challenge him based on his own jurisdictional rules.
Rav Yosef describes how his perspective on his own blindness and religious obligation shifted after hearing a teaching by Rabbi Hanina, changing his criteria for hosting a celebratory feast.
A man strikes another and Rabbi Yehuda Nesia rules that he must pay a Tyrian maneh in accordance with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
Rabbi Hanina attributes the untimely death of his son, Shivhat, to the fact that he cut down a fruit-bearing fig tree.
Rav Hisda sees date palms among his grapevines and instructs his sharecropper to uproot them because vines are more valuable.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua presided over a case involving the exchange of Agardemis coins at a specific rate.
Rav Hisda encounters Rabba bar Shmuel and asks him if he has learned a baraita regarding returning stolen items.
A man brings a slaughtered animal to Rav, who declares it non-kosher and exempts the butcher, leading Rav Kahana and Rav Asi to later comment to the man on the nature of the ruling.
Reish Lakish shows a coin to Rabbi Elazar for assessment and warns him that he is relying on his expert opinion, leading to a discussion on liability.
While sitting in a lesson, Rav Yosef physically turns his face away in disdain when Rav Huna issues a ruling he considers redundant.
Ravina delayed a legal authorization for twelve months because the creditor was a violent man who would not return property even if the claim was later overturned.
Shmuel takes advantage of a gentile's error by purchasing a gold bowl at the price of an iron one, adding a single coin to the payment.
Rav Kahana and Ravina engage in transactions with gentiles where they benefit from the gentiles' counting errors.
An incident involving a woman's eligibility for marriage comes before the sages, resulting in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permitting her to marry a priest.
A man informs thugs about the Exilarch's wheat, leading to its seizure and a subsequent ruling by Rav Nachman that the informant must pay for the loss.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda reports a ruling he made regarding an informer to Rava, who orders him to reverse the decision and return the money.
A man is coerced into showing and carrying Rav Mari's wine for thugs, and Rav Ashi exempts him from liability.
A man gives a deposited silver cup to thieves to save himself, and Rabba rules that he is exempt from reimbursing the owner.
A man entrusted with funds for redeeming captives gives the money to thieves to save himself, and Rava rules he is not liable.
Rava purchases grapevine branches from a sharecropper and defends the legality of the act when challenged by Abaye.
A dispute over a bathhouse is referred from Rav Ḥisda to Rav Huna and finally to Rav Naḥman, who resolves it using a specific legal principle.
Avuh bar Ihi bought a loft from his sister, but after a creditor seized it, Shmuel ruled he could not recover his money because no property guarantee was written.
Shmuel instructs his scribe, Rav Ḥinnana bar Sheilat, to include specific compensation clauses in deeds of sale if the parties agree.
The Gemara reports that Shmuel would regularly collect payments from buyers for land enhancements to satisfy creditors.
The Sages send Rav Sheshet's objection to Rabbi Abba bar Zavda, who dismisses it as simple, prompting Rava to argue that it is actually very deep.
An incident occurred in Pumbedita where a court ruling was challenged by Sages, leading to a sharp exchange between Rav Yosef and Abaye regarding the validity of the objection.
Rav Nahman recalls witnessing a public announcement by the judges in Mar Shmuel's court during his childhood regarding the return of found deeds.
Shabbtai son of Rabbi Marinus pledged a wool cloak to his daughter-in-law but denied it when her marriage contract was lost, only to be contradicted by witnesses.
Rav Yehuda follows Shmuel through the grain market and asks him about the law regarding a found purse.
Rava follows Rav Naḥman through the tanner's market and asks about the status of a found purse.
Rabbi Ami finds a purse of dinars and is seen by a Roman who, noticing his fear of the law, tells him to keep the find for himself.
Raḥava approaches Rav Yosef to ask if he may use orphan money in his possession, prompting a legal challenge from Abaye.
While sitting before Rabba, Abaye throws a clod at some goats, leading Rabba to rule that Abaye has now initiated the act of returning a lost item and must complete it.
Shmuel rent his garment in mourning for a Sage who had explained a single specific law to him, demonstrating his definition of a primary teacher.
During the time of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, students abandoned the Mishna for the Talmud, prompting him to publicly teach that they should return to prioritizing the Mishna.
The Sages consult the experts of the school of Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Oshaya to determine if two baraitot were originally taught as a single unit.
Rav Sheshet rules on a case in Neharde'a regarding a captive's property, but Rav Amram challenges his textual proof, leading to a sharp verbal exchange.
The Gemara cites a brief incident where a jug burst due to the expansion of grain during the rainy season to support a physical claim.
Rabbi Shimon challenges his father, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, for teaching a law differently in his old age than he had taught it in his youth.
Levi searches through his collection of baraitot and finds a text supporting the view that money effects acquisition in the context of consecrated property.
A man selling silk strips sets a price, and a buyer calculates whether the price constitutes exploitation.
A man selling jewelry sets a price, and a buyer calculates the exploitation involved.
A Tanna recites a baraita regarding the redemption of non-kosher animals before Rabbi Elazar, who then questions the logic of the baraita's exclusions.
Rav Kahana recounts sitting in the study hall and hearing Rav repeat a cryptic phrase about gourds, which he later asks the students to explain.
A man sells land without a guarantee and, seeing the buyer's distress, promises to compensate him if the land is seized, leading to a rabbinic discussion on the validity of such a promise.
A dying man writes a divorce for his wife to spare her legal complications but sighs in grief, leading his wife to promise she will remain his if he survives.
A man sells land with a guarantee for high-quality reimbursement, but after his best land is sold, the rabbis debate whether he must provide his remaining best land or only intermediate quality.
Rav bar Shabba pledges wine to Rav Kahana if a debt isn't paid on time, leading Rav Pappa to consider if the laws of asmakhta apply to movable goods.
Ravina acted in a case by removing the value of consumed produce from a lender.
Rav Ashi performed a legal action regarding the property of orphans.
Mar son of Ameimar describes to Rav Ashi how his father would record projected profits in loan documents but would later reduce the debt if the borrowers reported that no profit was actually made.
A business document involving the late Rav Ilish is brought before Rava, who interprets its ambiguous terms favorably to ensure no prohibition of interest was violated.
Rav Menashya bar Gadda unilaterally divides offspring from a joint venture and is rebuked by Abaye for doing so without proper authorization.
Rav pays donkey drivers to bring wheat from a cheaper market (Kafri) to Sura, assuming the risk of transport to avoid usury issues.
The Rabbis accuse Rava of taking interest by waiting longer to collect from sharecroppers, but he argues his method is actually more ethical than theirs.
Rav Se’oram would press people who behaved improperly into service as Rava's sedan chair carriers, an act Rava justified with a baraita.
A man acting as an agent for his father-in-law pays for jewelry whose price then drops, leading to a dispute brought before Rav Pappa regarding which price applies.
A Tanna recites a law regarding laborer wages before Rav, who corrects him by citing a different ruling from his uncle, Rabbi Ḥiyya.
A man sells a donkey but remains unpaid by one dinar, leading him to repeatedly seek payment and prompting Rav Ashi to deliberate on whether the sale is finalized.
A man took a donkey to sell it on the condition that he would return it if unsuccessful, but the donkey was injured during the return journey, leading to a legal dispute.
A man breaks a barrel in the Mehoza market and Rava instructs him to bring witnesses to prove it was an accident.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi proposes to Rabbi Elazar's widow but is rejected because she considers him spiritually inferior to her late husband.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, inspired by Rabbi Elazar's suffering, accepts thirteen years of physical ailments upon himself.

Passage B features a distinct set of actors (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Yishmael) and a specific dialogue-based encounter that evaluates the preceding events, constituting a separate narrative unit.
Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta, being obese and hot, sits on a rock and asks his daughter to fan him for a reward.
During the intense heat following his circumcision, Abraham sends Eliezer to find guests and eventually goes himself, leading God to send angels to visit him.
The members of Rav Pappa bar Abba's household approached Rav Pappa with two legal questions, and he provided them with restrictive rulings.
Rav finds a hidden scroll in Rabbi Hiyya's house containing a radical ruling by Isi ben Yehuda and expresses his concern that it would destroy people's livelihoods.
A man borrows an ax that breaks and Rava tells him to bring witnesses to be exempt from payment.
A man borrows a pail that breaks and Rav Pappa rules he is exempt if he brings witnesses of proper use.
The Rabbis attempt to use Rava's ruling to exempt themselves from liability to him, causing Rava to become angry and refute them.
A baraita alludes to a tragic incident involving a man who took his mezuza with him when vacating a rented house.
Ravina writes a large sum in his daughter's marriage contract and refuses the groom's family's request for a formal act of acquisition to solidify it.
A man on his deathbed instructs his heirs to give a sum to his daughter, leading to a rabbinic inquiry into his linguistic intent.
A sharecropper promises a high penalty if he neglects land, neglects a third of it, and the Sages of Nehardea rule on his liability.
A sharecropper plants wheat instead of sesame, and Rav Ashi rules that he doesn't get extra credit for saving the land's strength because owners prefer immediate profit.
A sharecropper plants wheat instead of sesame and produces a surplus, leading to a rabbinic disagreement over how to split the extra profit.
A man's wine turned sour after harvest, and Rav Ashi ruled that he could not pay his lease with it because the damage occurred to the product, not the land.
Rav Yehuda and Ravin bar Rav Naḥman, who owned adjacent fields, agreed to share the fruit of their trees that leaned over each other's boundaries.
Rabbi Abba meets the students of Rav and they exchange different interpretations of biblical blessings regarding the location of one's house and property.
Rav visits a cemetery and performs a ritual or inspection to determine that ninety-nine out of a hundred people died due to the evil eye.
A planter stipulates he will leave if he ruins the vineyard, and when he does cause a loss, Rav Yehuda and Rav Kahana debate his right to compensation for existing enhancements.
A planter requests his share of a field's enhancement so he can move to the Land of Israel, and Rav Pappa bar Shmuel rules in his favor.
A man mortgages an orchard that withers halfway through the term, leading to a dispute over whether the wood is considered principal or produce.
A creditor and debtor dispute the length of a mortgage, and the creditor preemptively consumes the orchard's fruit while the case is pending.

Yehuda bar Mareimar, Mareimar, and Mar Zutra employed specific hiring strategies, such as hiring each other or using specific language with attendants, to ensure they did not violate the prohibition against delaying wages.
A man takes a slaughtering knife as collateral and is ordered by Abaye to return it because it is a vessel used for food preparation.
In Nehardea, goats ate someone's barley, leading the owner of the barley to seize them and receive a ruling from Shmuel's father.
Rava physically removed a pair of wool-cutting scissors and a book of Aggada from the possession of orphans based on the principle that such items are typically lent.
An incident occurred where the floor of an upper story broke, causing water from the upper resident's washing to leak onto the resident below.
Efrayim the scribe reports that when Rabbi Shimon's ruling was presented to King Shapur, the King offered him high praise.
Rav Adda bar Ahava's host asks if he can roast eggs laid on a Festival for the following Shabbat, and the rabbi clarifies the restriction.
The Gemara notes that Rav Asi would perform Havdala between the two days of a Diaspora Festival due to his personal uncertainty about their sanctity.
Ravina notices Rav Ashi is sad on Rosh Hashanah because he forgot to set an eruv tavshilin, leading to a discussion on whether one can be set conditionally on the holiday itself.
Rav Mari found an egg on a Festival morning and searched sixty houses to see if a rooster was nearby to permit the egg.
Rav Adda bar Ahava would circumvent the restriction on salting meat on a Festival by salting pieces one by one and claiming each time that he preferred the current piece over the previous ones.
Rav Tovi brings a bottle of teruma wine to Rav Yosef, who rules that he may bring it to a priest on the Festival.
The host of Rava bar Rav Hanan asks if he can crush mustard on a Festival; Rava bar Rav Hanan doesn't know and asks Rava, who permits it.
The Gemara notes that the wives of Rav and Rabbi Hiyya would peel cups of barley for their husbands on Shabbat, challenging a restrictive ruling on the matter.
Rav Sheshet hears the distinct sound of salt being pounded in his house on a Festival and concludes it is being done in a prohibited, non-tilted manner.
The Gemara alludes to a historical tragedy involving spiked sandals on Shabbat which led to their prohibition.
Rav Taḥlifa bar Avdimi issued a ruling following Shmuel's lenient view, prompting a sharp rebuke from Rav.
A man leaves a bequest of 400 zuz to someone on the condition they marry his daughter, and Rav Pappa rules that the phrasing allows the recipient to take the money without the marriage.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava rebukes Shimon the Timnite for missing the study hall on a Festival to protect his property from soldiers.
Rava appoints Mar Shmuel to lecture on hosting gentiles, and the Gemara notes the visiting habits of Marimar and Mar Zutra on Festivals.
Ameimar has his eye treated by a gentile on Shabbat, and Rav Ashi argues that Ameimar's blinking constitutes prohibited assistance in the act.
Rav Geviha teaches an ambiguous ruling at the Exilarch's house and is challenged by Ameimar regarding its practical meaning.
Rav recounts how he and Levi witnessed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi change his legal ruling on fish brought by a gentile between one evening and the next morning.
Rabbi Ya’akov bar Idi reports an incident where an old man in his neighborhood used a litter on a Festival, leading to a ruling by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Aḥi Shakkaya and Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak recount specific instances where they physically carried prominent rabbis on chairs between towns on a Festival.
The Gemara notes that Rav Naḥman permitted his wife Yalta to be carried on a chair on a Festival because she was afraid of falling.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sends a firstborn animal to Rabbi Ami for examination on a festival, but Rabbi Ami is stopped from doing so by an objection from Rabbi Zerika.

When Rava bar Rav Huna taught a lenient ruling regarding sifting flour at the entrance of the academy, Rav Nachman sent his students to tell him his 'kindness' was unwanted and the law was already established otherwise.
When a brick fell into the oven of Rabbi Hiyya's wife on a Festival, he permitted her to sweep it out so she could bake.
Rava instructs his attendant to roast a duck for him and feed the innards to a cat.
A dead mouse was found in Rav Ashi's spice-house, and he ordered it removed by its tail on Shabbat.
Rabbi Elazar misses a session at the study hall and later encounters Rabbi Asi to ask what was discussed in his absence.
A female convert who raised animals in partnership with her gentile brothers seeks a ruling from Rava regarding the firstborn status of the livestock.
Rabbi Elazar reports seeing Rabbi Yoḥanan in a dream, which he takes as a divine sign that his legal explanation of Rabbi Yoḥanan's view is correct.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sends a firstborn donkey to Rabbi Tarfon to determine the redemption value, and Rabbi Tarfon rules based on the owner's generosity.
When students report a legal ruling to Rabbi Yehoshua, he instructs them to go tell Rabbi Yishmael that he has erred and provides a counter-argument.
Rabbi Shimon reports an eyewitness account of a single goat that produced ten offspring within one year, allowing the owner to perform the animal tithe.
When the Sages asked Rav Huna a legal question, he sent them to Rav Ḥananel to confirm a specific tradition first, which they did.
When Ravin travels from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael and recites a halakha, Rabbi Yirmeya insults the Babylonians for their 'dark' and foolish reasoning.
Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha invites Rabba bar bar Ḥana to come and observe which animal corneas change after death.
In Rabbi Yehuda's locale, one man insulted another, who retorted by boasting that he never ate Sabbatical year produce.
A man rents a donkey with instructions to avoid a watery path, but the donkey drowns, leading to a dispute over the renter's honesty.
A man brought a firstborn with obviously uneven eyes to Rav Ashi, leading to a discussion between Rav Ashi and Ravina about why the man bothered to seek a ruling.
Rav Shimi bar Ḥiyya challenges his grandfather Rav on a contradiction regarding a person with two spines, leading Rav to clarify that the Mishna refers to a crooked spine.
When Rav Huna gestured to demonstrate the meaning of a specific eye blemish, Rav Yehuda became angry at the display.
An incident is cited where a man calling for 'lukyanei' was found to be extremely white, clarifying a definition in the Mishna.
Rav Pappa recounts how Rabba tested him on the status of a priest's daughter pregnant by a gentile and corrected his mistaken comparison to a Levite woman.
Rabbi Tarfon habitually returned redemption money to fathers, and the Sages, upon hearing of this, praised him for fulfilling the law.
Shmuel's father constructed a ritual bath in the spring and placed mats in the river in the autumn to facilitate his daughters' ritual immersion according to specific halakhic requirements.
Rabbi Elazar recounts seeing Rabbi Yoḥanan in a dream, which he interprets as a sign that his legal explanation is correct, and uses this to answer Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim.
It features a different set of actors (a tanna and Rav) and a distinct legal scenario (the harlot's hire), though it functions as a scholarly exchange which often borders on 'not_a_story'.

Ben Azzai claims intellectual dominance over all Sages except Rabbi Yehoshua, but Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that Ben Azzai's specific legal uncertainty stems from the fact that the laws were received traditions from the last prophets.
Rabbi Zeira recounts how he initially disapproved of Sages running on Shabbat until he learned of the religious merit in rushing to a lecture.
Rabbi Yoḥanan is surprised to hear of elderly people in Babylonia until he is told they spend their time in synagogues.
Abaye describes how he changed his personal prayer location after hearing a teaching about the importance of the place of Torah study.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi avoided the thirteen synagogues in Tiberias to pray specifically in the place where they studied.
Rav Sheshet would turn his face away from the communal Torah reading to focus on his own study of the Oral Law.
Rav Beivai bar Abaye attempts to find a time to catch up on his Torah portions but is twice corrected by other sages regarding the proper timing.
Rabban Gamliel's sons return late from a wedding and consult their father on whether they can still fulfill the obligation of Shema.

Rabbi Zeira challenges the claim that one who juxtaposes redemption and prayer is never harmed by citing a time he was forced to perform a task for the king, which Rabbi Yosei then reinterprets as a merit.
Rabbi El'a tells Ulla to greet Rav Beruna, noting a specific incident where Beruna's successful juxtaposition of redemption and prayer resulted in him smiling the entire day.
Berurya rebuts a heretic's mocking interpretation of a verse in Isaiah by pointing to the end of the verse.
Rabbi Abbahu explains to a heretic why the juxtaposition of certain psalms is not a difficulty for those who use the method of 'semukhin'.
Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi observes Rav's habitual practice of washing his hands and reciting a blessing before teaching Sifra.
Rabbi Yirmeya observes Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba extending the word 'Ehad' excessively during Shema and instructs him on the proper limit of intent.
Rav tells Rabbi Ḥiyya that he did not see Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recite Shema, only to be told that the Rabbi's act of passing his hand over his eyes was the recitation.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yoḥanan used to recite Shema while leaning on his back because his corpulence made other positions difficult.
Rav bar Shaba visited Ravina while he was reciting Hallel, but Ravina did not stop to greet him because he did not consider him sufficiently important.
A prayer leader repeats the word 'emet' twice while leading the service before Rabba, prompting Rabba to mock him for his excessive precision.
The Gemara discusses Rav's ritual order of prayer and phylacteries, eventually explaining a specific instance where he deviated because a messenger brought his phylacteries late.
The sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya travel to the villages and forget their studies, leading them to wonder if their deceased father is aware of their distress.
A man who spoke disparagingly of the deceased Mar Shmuel was immediately punished when a reed fell from the ceiling and fractured his skull.
Following the dispute over the Oven of Akhnai, the Sages gathered all the food Rabbi Eliezer had ruled pure, burned it in his presence, and excommunicated him.
When students laughed at Rav bar Shaba's legal interpretation, Rav Kahana rebuked them and affirmed the speaker's greatness and the validity of his reasoning.
Rav Giddel sits at the gates of the women's mikveh to instruct them, and when challenged by the Sages, he claims he is immune to temptation.
Rabbi Yoḥanan sits at the gates of the immersion site so that women will see his beauty and have beautiful children.
A lenient ruling regarding immersion is passed secretly from Nahum to Rabbi Akiva to Ben Azzai, who then broadcasts it publicly in the market.
Rav Nahman creates a special jug for purification, but subsequent legal reports from Eretz Yisrael lead Rav Yosef to declare the practice (and the jug) obsolete.
Ravina and Rav Adda bar Mattana disagree on whether one can wear phylacteries to urinate and bring the question to Rava for a ruling.
Rabbi Hanina reports seeing Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi hanging his phylacteries, which prompts a legal discussion on the proper way to store them.
Rabbi Hanina testifies to seeing Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi perform various involuntary actions during prayer.
When asked about the status of flatulence during prayer, Rav Sheshet points to the students in the study hall who sleep and study together on mats without concern.
While Ravina was standing before Rav Yehuda of Difti, Rav Yehuda spotted feces and instructed Ravina to examine whether it had dried sufficiently to allow for sacred speech.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba questions Rav after observing him praying the Shabbat prayer early.
Rabbi Zeira, tired from study, sits at a doorway to honor passing Sages but instead receives and memorizes a teaching from Rabbi Natan bar Tovi.
Rav Avya misses Rav Yosef's lecture due to illness, and upon his return the next day, Abaye facilitates a conversation to ease the tension.
Elijah the Prophet appears to Rav Yehuda and provides him with ethical guidance and instructions on how to pray before setting out on a journey.
Shmuel recounts that he only ever prayed the Musaf prayer individually once, on the day the king's army arrived in Neharde'a and disrupted the community.
Rav Mordekhai accompanies Rav Shimi bar Ashi from Hagronya to Bei Keifei.
A parable describes a poor man who, after being ignored by a king's servants at the door, pushes his way inside to speak to the king directly.
Rabbi Yosei asks Rabbi Yoḥanan a legal question in Sidon regarding Havdala.
While Rabbi Zeira is riding a donkey and Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Avin follows on foot, they discuss whether a specific halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer.
Ravina encounters Mar bar Rav Ashi eating caper buds while discarding the berries and questions his legal reasoning for doing so.
An empirical experiment was conducted where flowers were removed from pomegranates and caper-bushes to see if the fruit would survive, resulting in a halakhic ruling based on the outcome.
When a student asks Rava about 'terima', Rava is initially confused by the term until Ravina clarifies it, leading Rava to recall and state the relevant law.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba reports seeing Rabbi Yoḥanan eat a salted olive and recite blessings before and after.
When a tanna named Shalman recited a ruling about combining bread pieces, Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak praised him with a pun on his name.
Rav Ashi reports seeing Rav Kahana's specific physical practice of breaking bread, leading to a discussion with Ravina about the optics of such an action.

Passage B is a distinct narrative unit featuring different actors (Rav Ami and Rav Asi) performing a specific action with a specific object (the eiruv bread) followed by their own explanatory response.
Rava bar Shmuel visits the House of the Exilarch and immediately breaks bread before salt is served, despite his own ruling to the contrary.
Binyamin the shepherd ate bread and recited a brief Aramaic blessing, which Rav subsequently validated as fulfilling his obligation.
Rav Huna eats thirteen large loaves without blessing, prompting Rav Nahman to tell him that such a quantity constitutes a full meal regardless of the bread's status.
Rav Pappa describes how his wife would cook turnips and then break the pot to neutralize their harmful effects.
Rav Pappa interrupted his own meal to act as the third person for his son Abba Mar's zimmun.
During wedding preparations for his son, Rabba bar bar Hana teaches his son meal etiquette, which is then discussed by other present sages.
Rav Aha enters a meal of Rav's students and corrects their assumption that he should be the one to recite the blessing.
Rabbi Eliezer enters a synagogue lacking a quorum and frees his slave so that the prayer service can proceed.
As children sitting before Rabba, Rava and Abaye demonstrate their understanding of God's omnipresence by pointing to the ceiling and the sky.
Rabba bar Rav Huna visits the Exilarch and recites a blessing with two themes, prompting a legal observation from Rav Hisda.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Hisda to teach Mishna, but Rav Hisda declines, claiming he has not yet mastered the laws of Grace after Meals.
Suriel the angel appears to Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha and gives him three practical warnings regarding morning routines and hygiene.
The Angel of Death speaks to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, warning him against certain morning habits and standing before women returning from a funeral.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda visits Rava's house and questions why Rava recites the blessing over spices before the light, leading to a legal clarification.
A man walking by the Euphrates is attacked by a lion and miraculously saved, leading him to recite a blessing at the site.
Mar, son of Ravina, is saved from thirst in a valley when a miracle causes a spring to appear.
When Rav Yehuda recovers from illness, his visiting colleagues recite a blessing that he accepts as fulfilling his own requirement to offer thanks.
Ameimar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi sit together and agree to each share a novel teaching, resulting in a series of instructions regarding dreams, the evil eye, and sickness.
Rabbi Bena'a recounts how he took a dream to twenty-four different interpreters in Jerusalem, and despite their different interpretations, every single one was fulfilled.
Ben Dama asks Rabbi Yishmael to interpret a dream about his cheeks falling off.
Rav Ashi recounts how he saw a goose in a dream and acted upon it, resulting in his appointment as head of the academy.
Rava and Mar son of Ravina perform symbolic physical actions upon seeing the ruins and earth of Babylonia to express its cursed status.
Ben Zoma sees a massive crowd on the Temple Mount and recites a blessing, using the occasion to reflect on the labor required for human sustenance compared to the ease of a modern guest.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna meet Rav Hanina on the road and inform him of the blessings they recited upon seeing him.
Ben Azzai follows Rabbi Akiva into a bathroom to observe his conduct and learn from him.
Abaye's mother raised a lamb to protect him from demons when he went to the bathroom.
The Sages gather in the academy at Yavne and begin a series of homilies honoring their hosts.
Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Elazar ben Ḥisma visit Rabbi Yehoshua and recount the homilies delivered by Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya in the study hall.
Rabbi Yoḥanan observes a man picking unripe figs and uses the encounter to understand why God might take righteous people before their time.
Rabbi Yannai sees a man giving charity publicly and tells him it would have been better not to give at all than to shame the recipient.
The Sages suggest Rava does not experience divine hiding because of his success, but Rava reveals he must secretly bribe the authorities.
Rabbi Ila overhears a child reciting a verse while climbing stairs and is moved to comment on the judgment of man.
Rav Kahana hides under Rav's bed to learn proper conduct, but his presence is discovered when he makes a comment about Rav's behavior.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is so distressed by a verse in Lamentations that the book falls from his hand.
An elderly Rabbi Ya’akov refuses his teacher's suggestion to stop his daily visits, arguing that seeing sages brings life.
While traveling together, Rabbi Yishmael questions Rabbi Akiva regarding the interpretive methods he learned from Nahum of Gam Zu.
Rabbi Elazar declines Rabbi Yoḥanan's offer to teach him mysticism until he is older, but by the time he is ready, Rabbi Yoḥanan has passed away.
The Elders of Pumbedita and Rav Yosef attempt to trade their respective knowledge of the Act of Creation and the Divine Chariot.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya rebukes Rabbi Akiva for engaging in Aggadic interpretation rather than focusing on complex laws of purity.
Shmuel finds Rav Yehuda weeping over the biblical verses describing the downfall of great scholars, fearing for the fate of the Sages.
When Rabbi Akiva entered the Pardes, the ministering angels tried to push him away, but God intervened, declaring him worthy of His glory.
Abba Elazar recounts an incident where a calf was brought to the women's courtyard so they could perform the laying of hands to satisfy them.
When Alexa died in Lod, the people gathered to eulogize him, but Rabbi Tarfon prevented them because it was a day of slaughter (associated with the festival).
Rabbi Asi reports seeing Rabbi Yoḥanan eat Samaritan slaughter, which leads Rabbi Zeira to resolve his doubt regarding whether a specific decree was accepted.
An incident involving a bird with a displaced windpipe was brought before the Sages, who ruled that any uncertainty in slaughter results in invalidity.
Rav Yosef disqualified thirteen animals after discovering his knife was notched upon completing the final slaughter.
Rav Pappa describes a case where one person binds another and diverts water onto him, causing his death, to define the legal status of direct force.
Shmuel's father repeatedly notched knives in various ways and sent them from Babylonia to the Land of Israel to receive a definitive ruling on which types of notches disqualify a knife for slaughter.
After Rav Huna rules stringently on a case where Rav Yehuda ruled leniently, Rav Yehuda becomes angry, leading Rav Hisda to advise Rav Huna on whether to retract.
When Rabbi Zeira arrived in Eretz Yisrael, he challenged Rabbi Ami's teaching on pinching, causing Rabbi Ami to be momentarily stunned before refining his position.
The Gemara records that Rabbi Hanina, even at the age of eighty, was physically capable of standing on one leg to remove and put on his shoes.
A bloody duck is brought to Rava's house, prompting a dilemma about whether its simanim were damaged before slaughter.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta enters a butcher shop and takes meat from a bull slaughtered with multiple cuts to demonstrate its validity, prompting a comment from Rabbi Zeira.
Rava, suspecting Rav Nahman was merely deflecting his legal objection, went out to investigate and discovered a baraita that confirmed Rav Nahman's position.
When Rav Kahana and Rav Asi question Rav on the specifics of an interruption in slaughter, Rav explains he was never bold enough with his uncle, Rabbi Hiyya, to ask for such clarification.
On the day Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya was appointed Nasi in Yavne, Rabbi Akiva expounded on the laws of ritual impurity in earthenware vessels.
After Rav's death, Shmuel encounters Rav's students and asks them to clarify Rav's ruling regarding an animal in danger of imminent death.
An animal with a suspected predator wound is brought to Rabba, who begins inspecting it from the outside until Abaye challenges him with his own legal ruling.
Rabba's wife (daughter of Rav Hisda) questions him for buying meat from an animal he himself permitted, and he explains why it doesn't look like a conflict of interest.
Rabbi Elazar consistently refused gifts and invitations from the Nasi's household, citing the verse that one who hates gifts shall live.
While in a bathhouse, Levi sees a man strike his head and remarks that the man's brain tissue has been fatally compromised.
Rav Dimi bar Yitzḥak asks Rabbi Yehuda for a physical demonstration of a spinal boundary; after Rav Dimi brings a kid for the purpose, Rabbi Yehuda decides to teach him the verbal tradition instead.
Ulla recounts how Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi was inspecting an injured bird but was interrupted by a messenger from the Nasi and left before Ulla could see the conclusion.
When Rav Ashi intends to rule a lung with an extra lobe as non-kosher, Rav Huna Mar bar Avya informs him that such a feature is common in field-grazing animals, leading to a kosher ruling.
Rav Neḥemya son of Rav Yosef physically examined a lung by inflating it in tepid water to check for leaks.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi pass through the Tiberias market and observe lungs with hard growths without objecting to their sale.
A needle is found in a lung's bronchus and brought to the Sages, who refuse to issue a ruling because it conflicts with their established traditions.
Mar son of Rav Yosef intends to rule a liver with a needle as treifa until Rav Ashi challenges him with a logical comparison to flesh.
Rav Ashi recalls Rav Kahana explaining how a date pit found in a gallbladder arrived there via the connecting ducts.
An anonymous Babylonian man travels to Eretz Yisrael specifically to verify legal traditions from Rabbi Abba.
When Rava is about to declare an animal non-kosher because test perforations don't match, his son Rav Mesharshiyya rubs the tissue until they match, leading to a kosher ruling.
A ewe in Rav Chaviva's house was observed dragging its legs, leading Rav Yeimar and Ravina to debate whether the cause was rheumatism or a spinal injury.
A fox clawed a ewe in the bathhouse of Beit Hini, and the case was brought before the Sages to determine if it was a tereifa.
Rav Ashi's duck entered a reed thicket and emerged with blood on its throat, leading Rav Ashi to evaluate its status.
Rav Ashi recalls a case brought before Rav Kahana involving a lung that looked like a shriveled date.
The hunters of the house of Yosef would kill animals by striking the sciatic nerve and sought a ruling from Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira on whether this rendered the animal a tereifa.
The hunters of Rav Pappa bar Abba killed animals by striking the kidney and were told by Rabbi Abba that they cannot add to the list of tereifot.
Rabbi Ḥana the money changer recounts how Rabbi Yoḥanan came to him to borrow a specific coin for a measurement and prevented Ḥana from standing up in his honor.
Ze’eiri travels to Neharde’a and sends a message back to the Sages retracting his previous legal ruling as an error.
Rabbi Simai and Rabbi Tzadok travel to Lod and stop in Ono, where they issue a legal ruling.
Rabbi Abba finds Rav Yirmeya bar Abba inspecting birds and they engage in a legal debate regarding Rav's rulings.
Passage B describes a specific event involving a ewe in a neighborhood and a medical intervention, which prompts a response from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, distinct from the hen incidents in Passage A.
An animal with two ceca is brought to Ravina, who rules it a tereifa based on Rav Huna's principle.
Rav Ashi intends to rule an animal with a specific tube a tereifa until Rav Huna Mar bar Hiyya informs him it is common in wild animals.
Mar bar Rav Ashi tries to permit an animal with a tube based on a previous precedent, but is corrected by Rav Oshaya.
Natan bar Sheila, the head butcher of Tzippori, testifies before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi regarding the status of an animal with two intestines.
Rabbi Abbahu recounts how he once ate a shekel of asafoetida and would have lost his skin to fever had he not immediately immersed in water.
A duck in Mar Shmuel's house had a gizzard that wouldn't peel until they placed it in the sun to soften it.
Rav Adda bar Shimi challenges a tradition about the raḥam bird by citing an incident where one hissed in a field and was immediately killed by a falling stone.
Ravina asks his mother to hide worms in his fish so he can eat it, leading to a legal challenge from Rav Mesharshiyya.
Avimi arrives from Bei Ḥozai carrying a baraita to challenge the current legal discourse.
Ulla rebukes Rav Yehuda's challenge by expressing extreme reverence for the deceased Rav and Shmuel while maintaining his own legal position.
While Rav Yosef is reciting traditions before Rav Huna, a colleague challenges his accuracy, leading Rav Yosef to react in anger before explaining the legal distinction that resolves the conflict.
When Rabbi Zeira arrives in Eretz Yisrael, Rav Asi confirms his teaching but describes how Resh Lakish once sat in silence waiting for Rabbi Yohanan to retract, leaving his own opinion unknown.
Rav Yehuda is silenced by Ulla in a legal debate, but after Ulla leaves, Rav Yehuda reflects on why he didn't offer a specific resolution and concludes his silence was justified.
Mar bar Rav Ashi recalls standing before his father when a bird was brought for inspection and Rav Ashi examined its sinews.
A case of soft sinews covering a broken bone was brought before Rabba, who ruled the animal permitted.
Rabbi Abba instructs his servant to carefully match the physical characteristics of mules before hitching them to his wagon to ensure they are of the same maternal species.
Rav Naḥman informs Rav Ashi that Ameimar actually permitted the consumption of the fat of forest goats, treating them as undomesticated animals.
Ya’akov the heretic challenges Rava regarding the covering of blood for domesticated animals, and Rava refutes him using a verse comparing blood to water.
Rav Eina teaches a law regarding covering blood on Shabbat at the Exilarch's gate, prompting Rabba to mock him and order his interpreter silenced.
Rabbi Akiva recounts traveling with Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua to a meat market to buy animals for a wedding, where he posed a question to them.
The Gemara describes the differing physical practices of Rabba, Rabbi Yoḥanan, and Rabbi Asi regarding how they removed forbidden fat from kidneys.
Ulla visits Rav Yehuda, who opens wine barrels for him that had already been sold to a storekeeper.
On the eve of Yom Kippur, ravens drop meat, and Rav Kahana permits Rav Nahman to eat it.
Rav Hiyya bar Avin loses meat in a wine cellar and is permitted to eat it by Rav Huna after identifying it through visual recognition.
Rav Hanina Hoza'a loses a side of meat and is permitted to eat it by Rav Nahman based on visual recognition.
Rav Natan bar Abaye loses ritual blue wool and is permitted to use it by Rav Hisda after identifying it.
An incident is recounted where a goat was roasted with forbidden fat in the synagogue of Maon, and Rabbi Yoḥanan was consulted to determine its permissibility.
When forbidden fat fell into a pot of meat, Rav Asi proposed measuring the pot's absorption toward the nullification ratio, but the Rabbis corrected him.
A man brought a mixture to Rabban Gamliel, who ruled leniently by citing an even more lenient precedent from his father.
A man brought a mixture to Rabbi Shimon, who ruled based on his father's precedent using specific ratios.
Rav publicly challenges Rabba bar bar Hana's ruling by appointing a disseminator to announce a contrary position to the masses.

Rava explains a legal ruling by citing a historical incident where, due to religious persecution, a message was sent from the Land of Israel to inform the community that Yom Kippur would coincide with Shabbat.
Rabbi Elazar poses a legal question to Rabbi Asi specifically to remind him of a tradition Asi had forgotten, eventually prompting him by recalling how Asi used to recite it before Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Rabba bar bar Hana observes Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi eating fruit without washing their hands and notes they did not offer him any.
Rabbi Tzadok is given a small amount of food and chooses to eat it with a cloth outside of the Sukka.
Rav Huna bar Seḥora feeds a piece of meat directly to Rav Hamnuna while the latter is standing before him.
Rabbi Elazar instructs his attendant to tear an udder before roasting it so that he may eat it.
Passage B is a distinct narrative involving Rabbi Elazar, Ze'eiri, and Rav Yitzḥak bar Avudimi investigating the origins of Rav's ruling, whereas Passage A is the actual event of Rav in Tatlefush.
Rav arrives in Tatlefush, overhears a woman asking how much milk is needed to cook meat, and decides to stay in the town to teach them the law.
Rav Safra returns to Eretz Yisrael and asks Rabbi Zerika about cooking liver, who responds by describing a visit he made to the house of Yehuda.
Abaye cites an incident where a bowl in Rabbi Ami's house cracked after salting meat, revealing absorbed blood.
A young bird falls into a jug of kutaḥ, and Rav Hinnana permits it, earning praise from Rava for his discernment.
The Gemara describes how Shmuel would throw bread contaminated by meat-blood to his dog, while Rav Huna would give it to his attendant.
A certain elder approaches Rabbi Elazar to resolve a legal dilemma by citing a tradition from Rabbi Yoḥanan regarding the validity of slaughter for impurity.
Rav Oshaya travels to Eretz Yisrael and debates Rabbi Ami over the correct context of a ruling by Rabbi Yohanan, a dispute eventually clarified by the arrival of Ravin.
Rabbi Yehuda recounts how he challenged Rabbi Akiva's ruling on fat by citing Akiva's own teaching on endives, leading Akiva to retract and change his position.
Rabbi Asi misses a session at the study hall, encounters Rabbi Zeira, and asks him to review the day's teachings to help resolve a legal difficulty.
A Levite was snatching priestly gifts from children, and when Rav was informed, he rebuked the Levite's greed while noting the legal complexity of taxing Levites.
Ulla habitually gives priestly gifts to the daughters of priests, prompting Rava to challenge the legality of this practice using a baraita regarding meal offerings.
Rava and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak fined individuals who refused to give priestly gifts by seizing their property.
Levi sowed crops in Kishar and, finding no poor people to collect the gleanings, consulted Rav Sheshet on how to proceed.
When a sack of coins was brought to the study hall for students, Rabbi Ami rushed to take it for himself (or for distribution).
Upon arriving in Eretz Yisrael, Isi bar Hini is corrected by Rabbi Yoḥanan regarding his terminology and his disrespectful manner of referring to the sage Rav.
Rav Huna cites a specific historical incident where Rav traveled to Damharyia and performed a physical act to settle a legal dispute.
Rav Anan points to the physical practice of Shmuel, who would enter and exit through the partially earth-filled gateways of Neharde'a without them being locked.
Upon arriving in Neharde'a, Rav Nahman ordered the removal of earth that was blocking the city gates so that they could be functional for locking.
In a specific crooked alleyway in Neharde'a, the authorities applied the stringencies of both Rav and Shmuel, necessitating the installation of doors.
Rav Yosef recalls an incident in a shepherds' village where an alleyway terminated in a backyard and Rav Yehuda ruled that no additional halakhic measures were required.
Mareimar used to close the alleyways of Sura with nets due to concerns about the river.
The residents of Sura placed a rolled mat in a crooked alleyway to permit carrying, but Rav Hisda ruled that their action did not satisfy the requirements of either Rav or Shmuel.
When Rabbi Zakkai recites a baraita regarding the status of the area between side posts, Rabbi Yoḥanan rejects the teaching and tells him to go teach it elsewhere.
Rav Yosef forgot his learning due to illness, and his student Abaye reminded him of a legal principle Rav Yosef himself had previously taught.
Rabbi Yoḥanan cites an incident where Rabbi Yehoshua traveled to study with Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri to clarify a legal point about partitions.
Rav Aḥa encounters the students of Rav Ashi and inquires about their teacher's ruling regarding doorframe markings.
Rav Yosef recalls an incident where Rav Yehuda permitted a courtyard breached by a sea inlet using only a single upright board.

Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel debated for two and a half years whether it is better for man to have been created, finally concluding that it is better not to have been created, but since he is, he must act righteously.
The Gemara mentions a specific balcony at the house of Bar Ḥavu over which Abaye and Rava disagreed.
Rav Dimi recalls seeing Abaye's head positioned between the pillars of the study hall while Rabbi Yoḥanan was teaching, signifying Abaye's deep concentration.
Mar Yehuda visits Rav Huna bar Yehuda, observes people carrying in a garden not planted in rows, and questions the practice until Rav Huna explains he follows Rav Nachman's lenient ruling.
The Sages discuss how to permit carrying in a specific large yard in Pum Nahara by debating the placement of side posts relative to the town and a nearby river path.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish testifies before Rabbi Eliezer that his father's household used to purchase fish brine with second-tithe money.
The Gemara explains a contradiction in Rav's rulings by narrating how his arrival in Babylonia and observation of local eating habits caused him to change his mind regarding green grain.
Rabbi Yirmeya travels to villages and is unable to answer a question about eiruv until he returns to the study hall.
Rava, in a boastful mood, compares himself to Ben Azzai and invites questions, leading a sage to ask him about the measure of apples for an eiruv.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports an incident where Rabbi Meir was in Ardiska and a man approached him regarding an eiruv.
Rabba bar bar Hana recounts traveling with Rabbi Yohanan to eat the sweet fruits of Genosar, where the group members would each consume ten fruits.
Rava challenges Rav Nachman with a baraita regarding retroactive designation, and Rav Nachman remains silent because he had not heard that specific tradition.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba observes Rav praying early and confirms that Rav has thereby accepted the prohibitions of the Sabbath early.
Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok recounts how his family once celebrated their traditional festival when it coincided with the Ninth of Av, choosing not to complete the fast.
Rav Yosef, having lost his memory due to illness, is reminded by his student Abaye of a legal ruling that Rav Yosef himself had previously taught.
A group of Sages travel from Pelandarsin by boat and find themselves at sea as Shabbat begins.
Seven teachings delivered in Sura on Shabbat morning appeared in Pumbedita by that evening, implying a miraculous traversal of the Shabbat limit.
Neḥemya son of Rav Ḥanilai accidentally wanders outside the Shabbat limit while studying, and Rav Ḥisda asks Rav Naḥman to arrange a human partition to bring him back.
The Gemara records three instances where straw, fodder, and water were brought to Levi, Ze'eiri, and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya using human partitions.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled like Rabbi Elazar but later realized he was in the minority, subsequently justifying his decision as valid for emergency situations.
Rabbi Eliezer misses the study hall, meets Rabbi Asi, and asks what was taught, learning that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina laughs upon hearing Rabbi Ḥiyya's stringent ruling regarding iron partitions in a ditch.
Rabbi Yoḥanan recalls his eighteen-day stay at Rabbi Oshaya's academy, describing the extreme physical crowding of the students and the specific lesson he emerged with.
An anonymous person asks the people of Judea about the spelling of certain words and receives a pluralistic linguistic response.
A Galilean woman's attempt to invite her friend for milk results in a garbled, nonsensical sentence due to her accent.

Passage B describes a distinct, recurring habit of Rabbi Abbahu using enigmatic language in a domestic setting, whereas Passage A is a specific dialogue between the Sages and Rabbi Abbahu regarding Rabbi Elai.
The Sages ask Rabbi Abbahu where Rabbi Elai is, and he answers using a complex riddle about a priestly girl.

Passage B is a distinct narrative incident involving Rabbi Elai and a group of questioners, featuring a specific verbal exchange and a clever metaphorical response, which is independent of Rabbi Yehoshua's story in Passage A.
A student of Rabbi Eliezer was liable for death by fire, but the Rabbis spared him because he had served a great scholar.
Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was so engrossed in Torah study in the lower marketplace of Tzippori that he was unaware his cloak was left behind in the upper marketplace.
Rabbi Yoḥanan testifies that he personally saw the location of the Israelites' camp and describes its size.
Rav Safra questions Rava about the Shabbat limits of two cities, and Rava takes him out to show him submerged wall foundations that justify the measurement.
Mar Yehuda instructs the residents of Mavrakhta to move their eiruvin to a more advantageous spot, but Rava rebukes him for following a minority legal opinion.
Rav Hisda consistently refused to answer even simple dietary questions during the lifetime of his teacher, Rav Huna.

Rav Hisda issued rulings in the town of Kafri while his teacher Rav Huna was still alive. Ravina examines a slaughtering knife in the jurisdiction of his teacher Rav Ashi, leading to a confrontation and a debate over the propriety of his actions.
While visiting Meḥoza, Ravina is asked by his host to check a slaughtering knife, but he refuses out of respect for the local sage, Rava.
While sitting with his teacher, Ravina sees a man violating a law and shouts to stop him, later receiving his teacher's approval for acting in his presence to prevent a sin.
Two rabbis parting ways at a river ferry engage in a series of legal inquiries regarding intoxication and property.
Rav Hisda's daughter asks him why he does not sleep more, and he replies that there will be plenty of time for sleep in the grave.
Rabbi Yehuda reports an incident where Ben Nappaḥa owned five courtyards in Usha and the Sages ruled that only his actual residence affected the eiruv laws.
Abaye reminds Rav Yosef of a legal tradition that Rav Yosef had forgotten due to an illness.
Rav and Rabbi Hiyya are cited as having relied on their teachers' eiruv while studying in their academies.
Rabbi Elazar hears Rav Beruna teaching a law in Shmuel's name, asks to be shown where Shmuel is staying, and goes there to confront Shmuel with a contradiction, leaving Shmuel silent.

Rav Beivai corrects the Sages, explaining that Rav Yosef misattributed a law to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi because his illness caused him to forget that Rav Beivai had actually cited it in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava.
When a gentile superintendent refused to rent his domain to his Jewish neighbors, Rabbi Zeira ruled that they could rent it from the man's wife without his knowledge.
A similar incident occurred where a superintendent refused to rent his domain, and the neighbors sought a ruling from Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya.
