In the days of Mar Shmuel, a loaf of lentil bread was so unpalatable that when he threw it to his dog, the animal would not eat it.
Bonyos sends an ancient se'a measure from Na'usa to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who then measures its volume in eggs.
Rabbi Yehuda recounts how residents drew water from a channel running between Avel and Tzippori under the Elders' guidance, which the Sages later attribute to the channel's small dimensions.
After Rav Yosef forgets his teachings due to illness, his student Abaye reminds him of a previous ruling, leading Rav Yosef to recall and clarify his position.
The Gemara cites traditions that Michal the daughter of Saul wore phylacteries and Jonah's wife made pilgrimage to Jerusalem without the Sages objecting.
While Rav Ḥinnana bar Shelamiya was teaching a version of the mishna to Ḥiyya bar Rav, Rav overheard and rebuked him for teaching a minority opinion as if it were the law.
An incident involving an alleyway bounded by the sea and a garbage dump was brought before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who declined to rule on its status due to concerns that the boundaries might change.
Rav arrived in Apsetaya and, seeing a need for a religious safeguard, prohibited the residents from climbing even stripped trees.
A heretic insults Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya by comparing Jews to thorns, but the Rabbi retorts by showing the biblical verse actually refers to their protective nature.
Rabbi Tavla visits Meḥoza and observes people using a door bolt in a specific way without correcting them, implying its permissibility.
Rav Avya visits Neharde’a and stops a man from using a door bolt that was only tied with a flimsy reed.
In Rabbi Pedat's house, ten people would move a massive beam to secure the door, and he permitted it because it functioned as a utensil.
Mar Shmuel permitted his household to use a large mortar to secure a door on Shabbat.
Abaye is silenced by Rav Safra's legal objection and later brings the matter to Rav Yosef, who provides him with a rebuttal.
Rava realizes he made a legal error and appoints a public speaker to announce his retraction and the correct tradition.
When the exiles returned from Babylonia, they camped at a specific well and the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi permitted its use.
Rav Huna and Rav Ashi would habitually convene ten scholars to sit with them during judgments so that the responsibility for any error would be shared among the group.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna visit Rava, who questions them on their learning and their financial success.
King Josiah, fearing the prophecy of exile, commands that the Ark and other sacred vessels be hidden away.
When the academy needed a head, Rav Yosef and Rabba sought guidance from Eretz Yisrael, but Rav Yosef ultimately declined the position for twenty-two years.
A group of four sages held a competition to see whose legal reasoning could not be refuted, resulting in Abaye being appointed their leader.
After being silenced by Rava's legal objection, Rav Nahman realizes the answer only after Rava has already departed.
Shmuel commands Rav Mattana not to sit down until he provides a scriptural source for a specific law, which Rav Mattana then does.
Abaye reminds Rav Yosef of a legal tradition that Rav Yosef himself had taught but subsequently forgot due to his illness.
A woman repeatedly brings sets of witnesses who are proven to be liars until Reish Lakish rules that she has established a presumptive status of dishonesty.
When foreign speakers came before Rava for judgment, he appointed an interpreter to mediate the testimony.
The Rabbis cast their eyes upon Rava son of Rabbah bar Mari, resulting in him becoming a scholar in fulfillment of a verse.
Rabbi Akiva encounters Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua in the meat market of Emmaus while they are shopping for a wedding feast and asks them a legal question regarding multiple transgressions.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana swears that Rabbi Yoḥanan taught a specific halakha despite Rabbi Yoḥanan's own denial.
When Rabbi Elazar asks for clarification on a legal point, Rabbi Yoḥanan tells him to find it himself, leading Elazar to depart and successfully research the matter.
Rabbi Yannai reports a ruling from a group session, and when Rabbi Yoḥanan notes it is already in the Mishna, Yannai uses a metaphor of lifting a shard to find a gem to claim credit for the insight.
While Rav Safra is praying, a buyer attempts to purchase an item and, receiving no response, repeatedly raises his offer.
Rabban Gamliel weeps upon reading a verse he interprets as impossible to fulfill, until his colleagues offer a more lenient interpretation.
Joshua encounters an angel who rebukes the people for neglecting Torah study and sacrifices.
Students misunderstand Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's instruction to 'repeat' the Megilla as an obligation to study Mishna, until Rabbi Yirmeya corrects them.
Rabbi Yoḥanan recalls a statement he made as a child which he later verified with the Elders.
When Rabbi Zeira passed away, a eulogizer delivered a poetic lamentation connecting his life in Babylonia and Eretz Yisrael to the city of Rakkath.
Rav Ashi is sitting with his teacher on Purim as it grows dark and notices the other Sages have not arrived.
When the Egyptians were drowning in the sea, the angels wanted to sing, but God stopped them, saying His handiwork was drowning.
The students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai ask him why the Jews of Ahasuerus's time deserved destruction, leading to a dialogue about their participation in the feast and the nature of their idolatry.
Rabba bar Avuha encounters Elijah the Prophet and asks him which of the Sages' opinions regarding Esther's motives was correct.
Rav Hisda discovers Rav Hananel writing Torah scrolls from memory and informs him that while he is capable, it is rabbinically forbidden.
Levi bar Shmuel reads a Megilla before Rav Yehuda, an incident that continues onto the next page.
Rabbi Yehuda recounts how he read the Megilla as a minor before Rabbi Tarfon and the elders in Lod, who then dismissed his proof.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi relates that he read the Megilla as a minor before Rabbi Yehuda, but the Sages argued that his action cannot serve as a general proof.
The Gemara records that after the death of Rabban Gamliel, weakness descended upon the world, causing the transition from studying Torah while standing to studying while sitting.
Rabbi Hananya Kara recounts his personal distress and the specific permission he sought and received from Rabbi Hanina the Great to divide biblical verses for the sake of teaching children.
After Rabbi Hiyya insults Rabbi Shimon's voice, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi tells his son to point out Rabbi Hiyya's own inability to pronounce certain letters correctly.
The Gemara notes a priest in Rav Huna's neighborhood who, despite having runny eyes, was allowed to bless the congregation because the townspeople were accustomed to his appearance.
The Gemara mentions a one-eyed priest in Rabbi Yohanan's neighborhood who was permitted to perform the Priestly Benediction because he was a familiar figure.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi if he may sow land containing synagogue ruins, and Rav Ashi instructs him to purchase it from the town representatives to remove its sanctity.
Rami bar Abba considers whether he can demolish an old synagogue to use its materials for a new one based on Rav Hisda's ruling.
Rabbi Yehuda cites an incident where Bytos ben Zonin performed a conditional sale of his field under the guidance of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
Rabbi Zakkai's disciples ask him about his longevity, and he responds by listing his lifelong pious habits.
A baraita records that Rabbi Zakkai inherited 300 barrels of wine from his mother and left 3,000 to his sons, attributed to his piety.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua explains his longevity to his disciples by citing his lifelong habits regarding synagogues and the honor of students.
Rabbi Perida attributes his longevity to always being the first to arrive at the study hall.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha the secret to his long life and receives a sharp retort followed by a blessing.
On his deathbed, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha blesses Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to live only half as long as he did, explaining that the next generation will need its own leader.
Ravina and Rav Adda bar Mattana were questioning Rava when it began to rain, prompting them to move their discussion into the synagogue.
Passage B is a distinct narrative incident involving Reish Lakish and a specific scholar, serving as a thematic foil to the subsequent story about Rav Nachman in Passage A.
When a man who had memorized many texts died, Rav Nachman refused to eulogize him, arguing that he was merely a container for books rather than a true scholar.
Levi bar Buti stammers while reading the curses before Rav Huna, who then permits him to stop and let another reader take over.
Continuing from the previous page, Rabbi Akiva defends his ruling to Rabbi Shimon, leading to a later debate where Rabbi Yoḥanan silences Reish Lakish regarding the nature of Akiva's response.
Rabbi Yoḥanan silences Reish Lakish with an objection, an event later analyzed and contested by Rav Pappa and Rav Yosef bar Shemaya.
Ben Bukhri testifies in Yavne that priests are not required to pay the half-shekel, and Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai disputes his interpretation of the law.
The Gemara recounts how the Hasmonean kings, lacking gold, fashioned the Temple Candelabrum out of iron spits and plated them with tin.
An incident is recounted where the Temple Candelabrum was found to be slightly too heavy and was refined in a furnace until it reached the exact weight of Moses' Candelabrum.
Rabbi Yosei relates that God sent fiery models of the Ark, Table, and Candelabrum from heaven so Moses could see and replicate them.
The angel Gabriel dressed as a craftsman to demonstrate the construction of the Candelabrum to Moses.
Moses struggled to understand the form of the Candelabrum, the moon, and creeping animals until God pointed them out to him.
Rami bar Tamrei brings damaged phylacteries to Rabbi Zeira, who instructs him to have a child read the letter to determine its status.
Agra brings a Torah scroll with extra letters to Rabbi Abba, who rules that such errors can be corrected, unlike missing letters.
The Gemara mentions an incident where Rabbi Elazar recoiled upon realizing he was sitting on a bed that had a Torah scroll on it.
The Exilarch asks Rav Nahman to affix mezuzot to his new house, but Rav Nahman tells him to hang the doors first so the placement can be determined correctly.
Abaye reports seeing that the porticos in Rabbah's house did not have mezuzot even though they had doorposts.
Rav Pappa visits Mar Shmuel's home, observes a mezuza affixed to an entrance with only one doorpost, and questions the legal basis for this practice.
While Abaye is studying with Rav Yosef, his phylactery strap tears, leading to a ruling that he may not simply tie it back together.

Passage B features a different set of actors (Rav Aha and Rav Ashi) and a different proposed solution (sewing vs. tying) to the same legal problem, following the common Talmudic pattern of grouping similar incidents.
Rav Ḥisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna are observed praying the evening service while wearing their phylacteries.
Ravina observes Rav Ashi donning phylacteries after dark and questions him, leading Rav Ashi to explain he is doing so to safeguard them.
The Gemara records the different physical methods Rav Yehuda, Rav Hanina, and Ravina used to protect their ritual fringes when sending garments to be laundered.
Rav Yitzḥak, son of Rav Yehuda, describes or performs a chemical test to verify the authenticity of tekhelet dye using a specific solution and overnight soaking.
Rabbi Mani was careful to buy wool according to the stringencies of the baraita, and an old man told him that his ancestors did the same and succeeded.
Rav Yehuda would put ritual fringes on his wife's cloak and recite a blessing every morning, a practice the Gemara analyzes to determine his legal stance on women's obligations.
Rav Ḥiyya bar Rav Avya would specifically eat spices and fruit on Shabbat to ensure he reached the daily quota of one hundred blessings.
Rav Aḥa bar Ya’akov questions his son's choice of blessing, leading to a discussion on which blessings are appropriate.
Ben Bukhri testifies in Yavne regarding priestly contributions to the half-shekel, and Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai corrects his assertion.
A Tanna recites a ruling about disqualified offerings before Rav Nahman, who questions the logic and identifies the teaching as belonging to the school of Rabba bar Avuh.
When the Sages present Rava's legal proof to Rabbi Yirmeya, Yirmeya insults the Babylonians' intelligence, leading Rava to defend his reputation and the quality of his legal traditions.
Rav Aḥa bar Ya’akov would wave his lulav and declare that he was shooting an arrow into the eye of Satan, a practice the Gemara subsequently discourages.
Different groups of rabbis ate the new crop at different times based on their legal interpretations of its prohibition status.
Ravina's mother reports to him that his father followed a specific stringent practice regarding the timing of eating the new crop.
The Gemara cites an incident where wheat rained from the sky onto Adi the Arab, covering a large area.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalls how he and his fellow students would carry oil and towels across various domains to serve Rabbi Shimon while studying in Tekoa.
When Rabbi Abba suggests that a certain offering is scattered to be wasted, the Sages laugh at him and question the existence of such a practice in the Temple.
Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua debate the consecration of loaves for a blemished offering until Rabbi Eliezer is silenced by a counter-argument and concedes.
Rabbi Elazar explains that he saw Rabbi Yoḥanan in a dream and was thereby inspired to provide the reasoning for Rabbi Yoḥanan's legal position.
The Egyptian sorcerers Yohana and Mamre mock Moses for bringing 'straw to Aforayim' (magic to the land of magic), and Moses retorts that one brings merchandise to where it is in demand.
Rav Ḥilkiya bar Tovi followed a specific biennial plowing and sowing cycle which resulted in a doubled yield of high-quality wheat that he sold for fine flour.
Rav Yosef would hoe his orchard land extra thoroughly, which resulted in the production of exceptionally strong wine.
Ben Dama asks his uncle Rabbi Yishmael if he may study Greek wisdom since he has already mastered the Torah, and Rabbi Yishmael rebukes him using a verse.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perahya remarks on how his attitude toward holding high office changed once he attained it.
Onias and his followers travel to Alexandria and establish an altar for sacrifices.

Rabban Gamliel's court votes to nullify early Sabbatical year plowing restrictions, leading to a later exchange where Rabbi Abbahu is momentarily stunned by a challenge to the court's authority before providing a justification.
Following their encounter with a man drawing water, Ravina challenges Rabba Tosefa’a’s call for excommunication with a baraita, leading Rabba Tosefa’a to retract his statement.
A student of Rabbi Yannai who usually challenged him daily refrained from doing so during public Festival lectures to avoid potentially embarrassing his teacher.
Rav Ḥisda's wife adorns herself on the Festival, leading to a sharp exchange between Rav Ḥisda and Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana regarding whether old women may use cosmetics.
Rav Huna hears a man chiseling a millstone on the Festival and curses him for desecrating the day.
Ravina delayed a business sale during the festival and subsequently doubled his profit.
Ravina consulted Rav Ashi about collecting a debt from the people of Shanvata during the festival, and Rav Ashi permitted it because the debtors were currently available.
Rava visited the Exilarch's house where they prepared fish for him by pressing it sixty times, and he ate it.
Rav visited Rav Shapir and was served a fish prepared in three distinct ways.
Rav Huna has his crops harvested on the Festival, leading his son to challenge the legality of the act based on a baraita.
Rav harvests his crop on the Festival, causing Shmuel to become angry until the circumstances are clarified.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia performs two controversial actions on Shabbat, leading Rabbi Ami to express dismay.
Rav Ashi goes to cut his forest on the Festival and is questioned by Rav Sheila on his legal reasoning.
Rav Yosef moves wooden beams into his house during the day on the Festival, defending the lack of 'discretion' to Abaye by explaining the logistical difficulty of moving them at night.
Rav Pappa recalls how Rava tested his students with a contradiction between two mishnayot regarding bringing tools from a craftsman, and how they successfully answered him.
Mar Ukva, distracted by a legal case, fails to honor Shmuel as usual, leading Shmuel to rebuke him in a way that the Gemara defines as a one-day admonition.
A dog that ate the Sages' shoes was excommunicated, resulting in its tail catching fire.
Rav Shemen bar Abba observes Rabbi Yoḥanan cutting and discarding his nails in the study hall during the Festival.
Bar Hedya reports witnessing people laundering basins of linen garments in the Sea of Galilee during the intermediate days of the Festival.
When Rabba bar bar Hana was in mourning and considered canceling his lecture, Rabbi Hanina encouraged him to teach for the public's sake, leading him to seek an alternative method.
An anonymous student travels from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael to verify a legal tradition with Rabbi Abba, only to be told the tradition was reported incorrectly.
An incident is recounted where a leading sage refrained from removing his garment in mourning for his father because another sage intended to do the same out of respect.
Upon the death of the Nasi, Rav Hisda instructed Rav Hanan bar Rava to stand on a mortar and display his rent garment to the public.
Abaye observes Rav Yosef practicing mourning rites privately on Shabbat and questions him about the legality of the act.
Rabbi Anani bar Sason teaches a law about mourning at the Nasi's house, causing Rabbi Ammi to become angry that he did not attribute the source.
Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa teaches a law in the Exilarch's pavilion, leading Rav Sheshet to express anger over the lack of attribution.

It describes a specific public event where Rav Pappa authorized Rav Avya the Elder to teach a ruling, followed by a specific response from Ravina, which constitutes a narrated incident distinct from the later encounter in Sura.
Ravina travels to Sura and is questioned by Rav Haviva regarding a ruling he reportedly gave about mourning before Rosh HaShana.
At Rav Hisda's funeral, Rabbi Yitzhak prevented the Sages from placing a Torah on the bier and provided instructions on when to sew their mourning tears.
When Rava feared the waters of the Tigris, he had Bar Avin recite a prayer for their safety.
Following the death of Rabbi Yoḥanan, Rabbi Ami observed an extended mourning period, which Rabbi Abba noted was a personal stringency rather than the law.
Passage B describes a distinct event involving the death and eulogy of Rabbi Zeira, featuring different actors and a different narrative focus than the mourning of Rabbi Yoḥanan in Passage A.
When Ravin arrived from Eretz Yisrael, Rav Tahalifa met him in the leather market and defined a 'dargash' for him.
Following the sudden death of Rav Huna, the Sages are concerned until Zuga explains that sudden death is only a bad sign for those who haven't reached old age.
The maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rebukes a man for curling or growing his hair too long.
A man vows to be a nazirite if his grain pile reaches a certain amount, but when he goes to check, he finds the grain has been stolen or lost.
Rabbi Yehuda cites an incident where a man vowed naziriteship for the number of days in a solar year and died immediately upon completing the terms.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva's teeth turned black from the many fasts he undertook (likely in penance or intense devotion).
Rav Adda bar Ahava questions Rav Huna on who shaves his sons' heads, and upon hearing it is Rav Huna's wife Hoba, he curses her that she should bury her sons.
The Sages observe that Rabbi Yoḥanan lacks armpit hair despite his ruling against shaving it, and Rabbi Shimon bar Abba explains it is due to his old age.
A man who excommunicated himself from the property of Rav Yirmeya's son seeks a ruling from Rav Hisda, who dismisses the validity of the vow.
Mar Zutra Hasida would excommunicate himself before excommunicating a student to share the burden, and then dissolve his own ban upon returning home.
Ravina approaches Rav Ashi to act as an agent to dissolve a vow taken by his wife.
A woman complains to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about her husband's atypical sexual behavior, but the Rabbi tells her he cannot intervene as the Torah permits it.
A man comes before Rav Huna to dissolve a vow, and after a brief exchange about his intent, Rav Huna dissolves it.
A man comes before Rabba bar Rav Huna, who asks if he would have vowed had he been appeased by ten people, and then dissolves the vow.

Two separate incidents are related where individuals came before Rabbi Asi and Rabbi Elazar respectively to have their vows dissolved through regret. A woman comes before a rabbi who questions her about the circumstances of her vow and subsequently dissolves it.
The grandson of Rabbi Yannai the Elder comes to him to dissolve a vow, and after a brief exchange, the rabbi dissolves it.
Rav Kahana visits Rav Yosef and they engage in a verbal exchange regarding an invitation to eat.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei seeks dissolution for a vow after an incident where a launderer hit him.
Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana intended to publicly teach how to preemptively void vows, but Rava stopped him to prevent people from treating vows lightly.
In the days of King Shapur, a massive snake was fed thirteen stables of straw which it swallowed whole.
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi, while debating a law, both took oaths asserting that their conflicting versions of Rav's teaching were correct.
While Rabbi Yirmeya dozes, Rabbi Avin and Rav Yitzḥak sit before him and discuss Bar Padda's legal position regarding the redemption of consecrated saplings.
A midrashic expansion of the biblical account where angels swallow Moses for neglecting circumcision until Zipporah intervenes.
Abraham trembles when commanded to be wholehearted, and God takes him outside to show him he is above the stars.
A baraita records an incident where a father's incentive for the Paschal lamb resulted in his daughters outracing his sons to Jerusalem.
Rava instructs his family to keep his illness secret on the first day but to announce it publicly if his condition deteriorates.
When Rav Yosef fell ill and forgot his learning, his student Abaye taught it back to him to restore his knowledge.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi taught Rabbi Hiyya part of a tradition, then forgot it due to illness, leading Rabbi Hiyya to teach it back to him.
A father vows to prohibit his son from benefiting from his property after the son is caught stealing flax, leading to a legal discussion about the status of the grandson's inheritance.
Rabba bar Rav Huna questions his father for eating porridge with his fingers, and Rav Huna justifies it using a teaching from Rav.
Rabbi Yehuda recounts an incident where Rabbi Tarfon prohibited his students from eating eggs cooked with meat following a specific vow.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda are eating figs in a field when the owner arrives and questions them.
Rabbi Ḥama bar Rabbi Ḥanina eats figs in a field and tries to convince his reluctant attendant to join him by citing a legal precedent.
Rav Ashi sells his forest to a fire-worship temple and defends the legality of the sale against Ravina's objection.
The Gemara describes the habitual physical manner in which Ḥiyya bar Rav and Rabba bar Rav Huna would conduct the dissolution of vows.
Rabbi Abba questions Rav Huna on whether Rav was silent (accepting a ruling) or merely busy drinking when a law was stated before him.
Rav Ika bar Avin reports that Rav personally attended to and dissolved a vow for Rabba.
Rabban Gamliel dismounts his donkey and prepares himself formally to dissolve a man's vow.
The Sages dissolve a vow for the son of Rav Huna bar Avin and then rebuke him for having made the vow in the first place.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava testifies about a rooster that was stoned in Jerusalem for killing a human.
An anonymous elder approaches Rabbi Zeira to clarify that a specific ruling attributed to the Sages was actually stated by Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Eliezer.
Rav Kahana recounts asking the wives of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua about their conduct regarding examinations when their husbands return from the academy.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalls a deaf woman in his neighborhood who was so proficient in checking for menstrual blood that she examined herself and her friends.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok brings a question regarding the definition of 'after time' to the Sages in Usha.
Rabbi Yehoshua's students complain that his adoption of Beit Shammai's strict ruling is too burdensome, to which he responds that it is better to be burdened in this world than the next.
The Gemara cites a past incident where Rabbi Meir attributed a woman's blood stain to a specific external cause to maintain her purity.
Rabbi Hanina broke a piece of earth to facilitate a blood examination, prompting a sharp rebuke from Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei.
In the days of Rabbi Yannai, the Sages attempted to rule a woman pure in a specific case of a sandal fetus, but Yannai rebuked them for effectively 'purifying offspring'.
Rav Pappa offers a legal explanation to his teachers who laugh at its obviousness, leading him to conclude that one should speak up even at the risk of being mocked.
An anonymous elder approaches Rabbi Ami to provide the scriptural basis for a ruling previously cited by Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Balaam is blinded as punishment for questioning God's involvement in human conception.
The students of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai ask him a series of questions regarding the laws of childbirth and circumcision, and he provides homiletic and psychological reasons for them.
Rabbi Dostai answers a series of questions from his students regarding the differences between men and women, attributing them to the materials from which they were created.
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi cite historical incidents where infant girls were immersed in ritual baths due to early menstruation.
Rav Pappa poses a legal question to Rav Yehuda of Diskarta, who remains silent, leading Rav Pappa to attempt to resolve the matter himself.
Rav Shmuel bar Bisna travels between Abaye, Rava, and Rav Yosef to confirm a legal ruling before returning to Abaye.
Rabbi Zeira sends Rabbi Yirmeya to Rabbi Avin to hear an explanation of a ruling, and Yirmeya goes and asks him.
The Sages inquired of the baraita reciters to determine the scriptural source of a specific law and discovered that multiple traditions existed.
The Gemara cites an incident where a mother died and her fetus continued to move three times after her death to challenge a legal assumption about the order of death.

When people brought youths with delayed puberty to Rabbi Ḥiyya, he would command them to physically fatten or thin the youths to see if their biological signs would manifest under different physical conditions.
Rabbi Zeira travels to Eretz Yisrael to verify a legal tradition from Rabbi Elazar and discovers the ruling was a logical inference rather than a definitive tradition.
Rabbi Hanina reports a specific case of a woman in his neighborhood whose left breast developed before her right, serving as the sole exception to the general rule.
A blind man in Rabbi Yoḥanan's neighborhood would act as a judge, and Rabbi Yoḥanan notably refrained from stopping him despite legal precedents to the contrary.
When students laugh at Rabbi Zeira's seemingly illogical legal distinction regarding a wild chicken, Abaye rebukes them and explains the reasoning to protect the sage's honor.
After Marimar rules that the marsh hen is forbidden, the Sages observe its predatory behavior to confirm it is a bird of prey.
Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri challenges Rabbi Akiva regarding the status of spices, leading to a formal vote and conclusion by the Sages.
Rabbi Yitzḥak and the disciples of Rabbi Ḥanina rule according to Rabbi Yehuda, and Rav Shemen bar Abba reports this to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who then takes the matter further.
Rava describes how Job blasphemed via a tempest and was answered by God in kind.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Asi a legal question and is ignored, only to later overhear Rabbi Asi teaching the answer to others, leading to a confrontation.
A woman who found blood on her loom came to Rabbi Yannai, who instructed her to re-enact her weaving movements to see if the threads could have touched her body.
Rabbi Eliezer b. Rabbi Yosei reports that he issued a restrictive ruling in Rome which was later praised by the Sages in the South.
The Gemara mentions that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Judah HaNasi once attributed stains to specific external substances.
A woman brings a blood stain case to Rabbi Akiva, who rules her pure and explains to his surprised students that the laws of stains were not meant to be overly restrictive.
Shmuel recounts how he questioned seafarers to identify the substance 'eshlag' and they described its origin in the crevices of pearls.
Rav Yosef, having forgotten his learning due to illness, is reminded of his own previous rulings by his student Abaye.
A virgin married and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi granted her four nights within a year to attribute bleeding to her hymen.
Ravina delays his son's wedding to Rav Hanina's daughter to ensure compliance with Rava's ruling regarding the seven clean days after a marriage proposal.
Shmuel's father implemented specific physical solutions, like digging holes and laying mats, to ensure his daughters could immerse in the ritual bath despite seasonal mud and shallow water.
After being challenged by Rav Pappa regarding a ruling on hair washing before immersion, Rava publicly retracts his opinion through an interpreter.
While walking on a road, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi consults Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon regarding a woman's ritual purity status and later reflects on a specific question he neglected to ask.
The wise people of Alexandria travel to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥinnana to ask him twelve questions categorized into wisdom, aggada, ignorance, and behavior.
Three priests describe their small portions of showbread, and the one who uses a crude metaphor is investigated and found to be disqualified from service.
A man's habitual use of a specific phrase leads the Sages to identify his tribal lineage.
A man's habitual praise of the seashore leads to the discovery of his Zebulunite ancestry.
Rava instructs the residents of Meḥoza to remove leaven belonging to gentile soldiers from their homes because the residents' financial responsibility for it makes it legally theirs.
Students living in the fields ask Rav if they are protected from robbers when traveling to and from the academy, and Rav guarantees their safety only for the trip there.
A man threatened with death by a local lord if he does not kill another person seeks guidance from Rava, who rules that he must allow himself to be killed rather than murder.
Shmuel threatens pot merchants that he will publicize a lenient ruling allowing the use of old pots if they do not lower their prices after Passover.
An oven was smeared with meat grease and used for bread, leading Rava bar Ahilai to prohibit the bread entirely.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi how to prepare knives for Passover, and Rav Ashi reveals that he personally makes new ones, prompting Ravina to remark on the difference between the wealthy and the poor.
When asked about glazed vessels, Ameimar reports his physical observation of them 'sweating' liquid, leading him to prohibit them for Passover use.
When Ravin travels to Eretz Yisrael and recites a law, Rabbi Yirmeya insults him and all Babylonians for their 'dark' and confused traditions.
While Rav Pappa and Rav Huna are debating a legal point, their noise wakes up Rav Idi bar Avin, who rebukes them and explains the reasoning behind Reish Lakish's ruling.
Rabbi Yehoshua instructs his sons on the specific nights of Passover when they should and should not knead their dough with milk.

Passage B describes a specific historical debate between Baitos ben Zonin and the Sages involving a concrete proposal (using a mold) and a definitive rejection, distinct from the father-son dialogue in Passage A.
Rabbi Ile’a travels among the students of Rabbi Eliezer to find confirmation for a specific botanical ruling regarding Passover.
Ravina encounters Rav Aḥa searching for particularly bitter herbs and questions why he isn't using the preferred lettuce mentioned in the Mishna.
The Gemara begins to describe the specific practice of Mar son of Ravina's mother regarding the guarding of wheat for Passover.
Rav Pappi permitted the Exilarch's cooks to mash roasted grain into food, but Rava objected because servants cannot be trusted to be careful.
The Sages present a legal theory to Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira, leading to a disagreement where Yirmeya accepts the logic while Zeira rejects it, sparking a debate.
Rabbi Yehoshua married a priest's daughter, fell ill, and attributed his illness to Aaron's displeasure with the match.
Rav Kahana attributes his exile to his marriage to a priest's daughter, though others argue his exile to a place of Torah was not a punishment.
Rava intends to publicly explain the pronunciation of God's name but is stopped by an old man who points out that the name must remain hidden.
The residents of Ḥozai report their custom of separating challah from rice to Rav Yosef, who orders a public violation of the custom to correct them, leading to a legal challenge by Abaye.
Ulla glares at Rabba bar bar Ḥana for a perceived misattribution of a teaching, leading to a tense exchange that Rav Yosef later characterizes using a verse from Proverbs.
Rav Pappa recounts how Rava tested the students with a legal contradiction regarding bringing vessels from a craftsman, and how they successfully resolved it.
Jacob attempts to reveal the end of days to his sons but loses his prophetic inspiration, leading to a dialogue about their faith and the origin of a liturgical response.
Owners of sycamore trees in Jericho consecrated their timber to the Temple to prevent it from being seized by powerful men.
The Temple Courtyard is described as crying out to expel corrupt priests and welcome worthy ones.
During the time of Hillel, an elderly man was crushed to death by the massive crowds in the Temple courtyard on Passover.
A Tanna recites a baraita before Rav Yitzḥak bar Avdimi, who points out a logical flaw in the sequence of the laws and suggests a corrected version.
On Shavuot, Rav Yosef orders a special calf to be prepared and remarks that without the Torah, he would be no different from any other man in the market.
During a legal debate, Rabbi Eliezer becomes so incensed by Rabbi Akiva's refutation that he curses him to die by slaughter, leading Akiva to beg for mercy.
Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak sit together on a porch and discuss the legal consequences of accidental transgressions involving sacrificial meat and marital relations.
Ravin the Elder prepares a dove wrapped in dough for Rav, who then comments on whether he will eat the breading.
Rava visits the Exilarch's home and refuses to eat a breaded goose until he verifies the breading did not absorb blood.
A young bird fell into a jug of dairy kamka, and Rav Ḥinnana permitted it, a ruling later praised by Rava.
A fish was roasted with meat, and Rava prohibited eating it with dairy because of the absorbed aroma.
Rabbi Oshaya refutes a heretic's claim that the exile proves God's abandonment by arguing that the dispersion is actually a protective measure.
A baraita records an incident where a father challenged his children to race to Jerusalem for the Paschal lamb, and the daughters arrived before the sons.
A Tanna recites a baraita regarding a Zava before Rav Adda bar Ahava, who challenges the validity of the text because a Zava cannot be ritually fit on her seventh day.
Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai describes how a Divine Voice rebuked Nebuchadnezzar's hubris by informing him of the vast distances of the heavens and his ultimate descent to the pit.
Rabba bar Rav Huna visits the Exilarch and, when presented with a table as Shabbat begins, spreads a cloth to perform kiddush.
Rav Anan bar Taḥalifa recalls witnessing Shmuel descend from his roof to the ground floor and repeat the kiddush prayer to satisfy the requirement of eating in the place of the blessing.
Rav Ya’akov bar Abba observes Rava reciting multiple blessings over wine during a meal and questions the necessity, leading Rava to explain his reasoning.
Rav Huna sees a man drinking water before Havdala and warns him that he is at risk of the ailment askara.
Rav Huna finds Rav reciting kiddush over beer and rebukes him by suggesting he is choosing a cheap drink to save money.
Abaye recounts how students crowded together on each other's knees to recline at Rabba's house, but were later told by Rav Yosef that they need not recline in his presence.
The Gemara describes how the mothers and attendants of Abaye and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak would physically intervene with extra cups to ensure they never drank in dangerous pairs.
Rava allowed his students to leave after four cups, and even when Rava bar Livai was injured, Rava attributed the injury to a different cause rather than the danger of pairs.
Ameimar reports an encounter with the chief of witches who provided him with a protective incantation against witchcraft.
Rav Dimi of Neharde’a was careful not to mark barrels with even numbers, and once a barrel marked with pairs burst.
The Gemara alludes to an incident where Rabba bar Nahmani witnessed someone being harmed after drinking an even number of cups.
The Gemara alludes to an incident where a man riding a donkey was targeted by witchcraft despite certain conditions being met.
A demon mother warns her son to avoid a specific tree that killed his father, but the tree eventually kills the son as well.
Rav Pappa enters a gentile woman's house to collect a debt and she invites him to sit on her bed, an incident used to explain a warning against sitting on such beds.
When a baraita praising certain people is recited, Rav Safra becomes joyful thinking it refers to him, but Rava clarifies it refers to more pious individuals like Rav Hanina and Rav Oshaya.
Rava specifically sought out beets and rice for his Passover meal because he heard Rav Huna mention them as examples of the two cooked dishes.
While sitting at the Seder as a child, Abaye noticed the table being removed and asked why, leading Rabba to conclude that Abaye's curiosity exempted them from reciting 'Mah Nishtanah.'
Mareimar inquires with the students of Rav Yosef and Rav Sheshet to discover that despite their blindness, they personally recited the Passover Haggadah.
Rabba would tell a joke to make the Sages laugh before beginning his lecture, at which point he would transition into a state of trepidation.
Ravina recounts how a congregation in Sura tried to silence a prayer leader for using an unfamiliar formula, until Mareimar intervened to support the leader.
When God decrees that Adam will eat the herb of the field, Adam weeps and pleads not to be equated with his donkey.
When Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei falls ill, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sends for his father's traditions, which Yishmael then transmits.
Abaye observes Rabba dozing during the eating of the matza and questions him, leading Rabba to define his state as 'dozing' to permit further eating.

After Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling on carobs, Yoḥanan remains silent, prompting a meta-discussion between Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yosei about why he didn't respond and whether he conceded.
Beloreya the convert challenges Rabban Gamliel with a biblical contradiction, and Rabbi Yosei the priest intervenes to resolve it with a parable.

Ulla arrives in Babylonia and informs the local scholars that the court in Eretz Yisrael intercalated Elul to ensure Festivals do not conflict with Shabbat for the sake of fresh vegetables and burial needs.
Rabbi Nehorai traveled to Usha on Shabbat to testify on behalf of a witness to the new moon.
Shmuel sees a ring with a protruding image belonging to Rav Yehuda and commands him to deface it.
Rav, Shmuel, and other sages would enter and pray in a specific synagogue in Nehardea that contained a royal statue.
Rabbi Ḥiyya sees the old moon still visible on the 29th and throws a clump of earth at it, telling it to hide so the new moon can be sanctified that night.
Rabbi Akiva travels to Arabia and discovers that the local population calls a ram 'yovela', clarifying a biblical term.
Rabbi Akiva recounts his travels to Galia and Africa where he learned local meanings for biblical terms.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi travels to coastal towns and learns that 'kira' means 'sale', explaining Jacob's purchase of a grave.
Resh Lakish travels to Kan Nishrayya and identifies the meanings of 'ninfi' and 'sekhvi' from local speech.
Rabbi Halafta and Rabbi Hananya ben Teradyon established Temple-style shofar customs in their respective cities, but the Sages later ruled that such practices were only permitted in the Temple.
Rabbi Zeira instructs his servant regarding the intent required when sounding the shofar for him.
Rav Ashi recalls how Rav Pappi would recite kiddush for his students and then repeat it for his tenants when they returned from the fields.
Rabbi Abbahu, facing doubt over the nature of the shofar's 'terua' sound, establishes a new combined sequence of blasts in Caesarea to ensure the obligation is met.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel instructs his attendant to sound the shofar during his private Rosh HaShana prayer, but Rava informs him that this is only done in a communal setting.
Mar Zutra errs in a legal ruling and consults Rav Yosef, who determines his liability based on whether the litigants accepted him.
Rabba bar Hana errs in a judgment in Babylonia and seeks a ruling from Rabbi Hiyya regarding his liability.
Rabba bar Rav Huna asserts his independent judicial authority during a dispute with the Exilarch's household.
Tanḥum son of Rabbi Ami arrives in Hatar and issues a ruling, but is rebuked by the locals for ruling in the presence of a more senior rabbi.
A man walking by recites a proverb about silence, and Shmuel identifies a biblical verse that mirrors the sentiment.
A man walking by speaks about the frequency of theft and divine punishment, prompting Shmuel to cite a supporting verse.
A man walking by recites a proverb about the righteous escaping pits, which Shmuel links to a verse in Proverbs.
A man walking by recites a proverb about accepting a court's judgment joyfully, and Shmuel provides a biblical source.
A man walking by recites a proverb about laziness, and Shmuel connects it to a verse in Ecclesiastes.
A man walking by recites a proverb about a trusted friend turning against him, and Shmuel cites a parallel verse from Psalms.
A man walking by recites a proverb about how love affects the perception of physical space, and Rav Huna provides biblical parallels.
Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai once conducted a cross-examination of witnesses by asking about the specific physical characteristics of the stems of the fig tree where the event occurred.
Rabbi Shimon cites an incident where Rabbi Akiva, while imprisoned, intercalated three years in a row.
Rabbi Yehuda cites an incident where King Hezekiah intercalated the year due to ritual impurity and subsequently prayed for forgiveness.
Rabbi Yoḥanan is distressed because Rav Shemen bar Abba was not present to be ordained when the opportunity arose.
Whenever Rabbi Abbahu visited the emperor's palace, the noblewomen would come out and sing a song of praise to him.
The Sages overhear three cattle herders describing seasonal signs to determine if the month is Adar, which ultimately aligns with the Sages' own calculations for intercalating the year.
Rabbi Yosei instituted specific communal regulations in the city of Tzippori regarding mourning customs and public conduct.
Rav Menashya bar Ute recounts asking Rabbi Yoshiya the Great a question about the consolation line while they were in the cemetery of Huzal.
Palti son of Laish places a sword between himself and Michal to ensure he does not touch her, remaining chaste until she returns to David.
Ravin reports that Rav Taḥlifa, who frequented the leather market, identified the 'dargash' as a leather bed, resolving a scholarly debate through personal experience.
When Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter, the angel Gabriel planted a pole in the sea which eventually became the site where Rome was built.
When asked about the High Priest's haircut, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi points to his son-in-law Ben Elasa, who spent a fortune to maintain that specific style as a visual reference.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi teaches a prohibition on Shabbat insulation but immediately defers when Rabbi Yishmael cites his father's contrary ruling.

A slaughterer caught selling non-kosher meat is disqualified by Rav Nahman, but after the slaughterer performs physical acts of penance, Rav Nahman considers reinstating him until Rava warns it might be a ruse.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel attempts to validate a gift deed signed by known robbers, but Rava corrects him, stating that Torah-level robbers are disqualified without a court proclamation.
Rav Zevid disqualified two of his tenant farmers from testifying after they were caught stealing small amounts of barley and dates.
A man hides witnesses in his bed canopy to overhear a debtor's admission, but the debtor later denies the seriousness of the statement.
A man hides witnesses in a grave to overhear a debtor's admission, but the debtor refuses to acknowledge them as formal witnesses.
A man known for his many debts publicly admits to owing specific people, but Rav Nachman rules the admission invalid as it may have been a lie to hide his wealth.
The Gemara investigates whether the scribes of Abaye and Rava are familiar with a specific legal requirement, and they confirm that they are.
A man distressed over his father's hidden inheritance is visited by a dream figure who reveals the money's location and that it is second tithe, leading to a rabbinic ruling.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak meets Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua and discusses a legal contradiction, leading to a display of the latter's self-defeating dialectical brilliance.
A case involving conflicting testimony about whether wine or oil was delivered comes before Rabbi Ami, who rules that the defendant must pay for the cheaper item.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi validates a case where witnesses disagreed on which floor an event occurred by combining their testimony.
The Sages of Tiberias send a letter to Mar Ukva regarding a complaint brought by Ukvan against his brother Yirmeya.
A blind man in Rabbi Yoḥanan's neighborhood served as a judge, and Rabbi Yoḥanan did not intervene to stop him.
A heretic challenges Rav Kahana on how a husband and wife can be secluded during her menstruation without sinning, and Rav Kahana credits the Torah's protection.
A heretic challenges Rav Idit regarding the divinity of Metatron, and Rav Idit provides a linguistic refutation.
When a heretic challenged Rabbi Yishmael on a verse, a laundryman asked for permission to respond and silenced the heretic with a parable.
Rabban Gamliel uses the emperor's physical distress over his distant son to refute the emperor's claim that he knows where God 'sits'.
A magus claims that the upper and lower halves of Ameimar's body belong to different gods, and Ameimar refutes him by asking how one god allows the other's waste to pass through his domain.
Rabban Gamliel physically strikes the emperor's servant to set up a demonstration using the sun to explain how the Divine Presence can be in many places at once.
While being mocked by a heretic, Rabbi Abbahu is approached by a student, and he uses the student's query to formulate a response to the heretic.
Ben Zakkai cross-examines witnesses in a murder trial by asking highly specific questions about the physical characteristics of the fig tree where the crime occurred.
Rav Kahana and Rav Safra are encountered by Rami bar Ḥama, who challenges their learning on Sanhedrin, leading to a sharp resolution and mutual respect.
Mareimar and Mar Zutra would support each other physically by leaning on one another's shoulders while reciting the blessing over the new moon.
After Rabbi Sheila publicly lectured that Joshua was personally sinful, Rav waited for him to leave and then appointed an interpreter to teach the public that Joshua was actually blameless.
Rabbi Eliezer cites a historical incident where Shimon ben Shataḥ executed eighty witches in Ashkelon on a single day.
King Shapur of Persia challenges Rav Ḥama to find a Torah source for the requirement of burial, and Rav Ḥama is unable to answer.
On his deathbed, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi instructed his disciples to only eulogize him in large cities rather than small towns.
People used dirt from Rav's grave to cure fevers and consulted Shmuel, who ruled the practice permissible because the ground itself is not forbidden like a corpse.
Rav Huna physically cut off the hand of a man who was known for habitually striking others.
Rav Hamnuna is searching for his lost oxen when he is met by Rabba, who uses the opportunity to pose a legal contradiction regarding idol worship.
Rabbi Zakkai recites a baraita before Rabbi Yoḥanan, who rejects the teaching as incorrect and orders him to teach it outside the study hall.
Ulla arrives from Eretz Yisrael and tells Rava he stayed in Kalnevo, leading to a discussion on whether mentioning the name of a place named after an idol is permitted.
The Gemara relates how Hezekiah's mother saved him from his father's attempt to sacrifice him to an idol by rubbing him with fireproof salamander blood.
Rav Hanina and Rav Oshaya would study the Book of Creation every Friday, resulting in the creation of a calf which they would then eat.
The Gemara records that the court in Lod used the entrapment method described in the Mishna to catch and hang an inciter named Ben Setada on the eve of Passover.
A woman tries to collect dust from under Rabbi Hanina's feet for sorcery, but he tells her to proceed if she can, as he trusts in God's exclusive power.
Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok and Rabbi Shimon of Akko provide eyewitness accounts of ruins and marked stones to prove that leprous houses actually existed in history.
The Sages gathered in the upper story of the house of Nitza in Lod, voted, and established the laws of martyrdom.
A man comes to Rabba for advice after a local lord threatens to kill him unless he murders someone else, and Rabba tells him to accept death instead.
A man confined another person's animal in the sun until it died, leading Ravina and Rav Aha bar Rav to dispute whether he is liable for damages.
Rav Yehuda corrects his father Rav Yeḥezkel's teaching of a Mishna, leading Shmuel to praise Rav Yehuda's sharpness.
Rav and Mar son of Ravina refused to let their sons perform minor surgeries on them to prevent the sons from accidentally violating the capital prohibition against wounding a parent.
Rabbi Yoshiya travels to the South to present three traditions he received from Zeira, but the local scholars only accept two of them.
The Gemara describes how the failure of the disciples of Shammai and Hillel to properly apprentice led to the proliferation of legal disputes and the fragmentation of the Torah.
The Gemara elaborates on the biblical account of Zedekiah son of Chenaanah's false prophecy to Ahab, explaining the supernatural cause (the spirit of Naboth) and how Jehoshaphat identified the fraud.
The Gemara describes how Hananiah son of Azzur came to issue a false prophecy by overhearing Jeremiah and applying his own logical deduction.
Ishmael boasts to Isaac about his circumcision at age thirteen, prompting Isaac to declare he would sacrifice his entire life to God.
Heretics challenge Rabban Gamliel to find a source for the resurrection of the dead in the Torah, Prophets, and Writings, and he eventually provides a verse that satisfies the requirement.
The Romans question Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya about resurrection and God's foreknowledge, leading to a debate over the interpretation of a verse.
Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yosei recounts how he refuted the Samaritan denial of resurrection by pointing out contradictions in their own version of the Torah.
Queen Cleopatra asks Rabbi Meir whether the dead will be resurrected naked or clothed, and he answers using the analogy of a grain of wheat.
A heretic challenges Rabbi Ami regarding resurrection, and the Rabbi responds with a parable about a king and his servants.
Geviha ben Pesisa engages in a sharp verbal exchange with a heretic who mocks the belief in resurrection.
Antoninos challenges Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on how the body and soul can be judged if they can each blame the other.
When Jacob attempts to leave after praying, God causes the sun to set prematurely so that the righteous man will stay at His 'inn' for the night.
Elijah the prophet appears to Rav Yehuda and provides a calculation for the minimum duration of the world and the timing of the Messiah's arrival.
King Shapur mocks the idea of the Messiah arriving on a donkey, and Shmuel retorts that the king's horses cannot compare to the Messiah's miraculous donkey.
A heretic asks Rabbi Abbahu when the Messiah will come, and the Rabbi responds that it will be a time of darkness for the heretic's people.
Rav Pappa accidentally used a disrespectful term for Sages and subsequently fasted to atone for it.
Jeroboam manipulates the righteous elders of Israel into signing a blank check of authority by seating them next to wicked men, eventually forcing them to support idolatry.
Amon commits incest with his mother, who then rebukes him by arguing that the shame outweighs the pleasure.
Jehoiakim claims he has no need for God's light because of his gold, but his advisors remind him that the gold also belongs to God.
The ministering angels attempt to destroy Micah for his idolatry, but God stops them because Micah provided food for travelers.
Ten men visit the prophet Ezekiel and argue that since God 'sold' the Jewish people into exile, He no longer has a claim over them.
A heretic asks Rabbi Hanina if he knows Balaam's age at death, and the Rabbi deduces it from a verse in Psalms.
The Gemara notes that when Rav Yehuda would remove his shoe to pray for rain, it would fall immediately, unlike the prayers of later generations.
Hushai the Archite meets David in mourning and challenges him on his marriage to a 'beautiful woman' (yefat toar), leading to a discussion on biblical exegesis.
After Rabbi Yosei teaches the methods of theft used in Sodom, thieves in Tzippori immediately use those methods, leading the townspeople to blame the Rabbi.
Rav Kahana washes his hair and sits before Rav, who quotes a verse that Rav Kahana mistakenly interprets as a curse upon himself.
Rabbi Hagga, while climbing the stairs of a study hall, hears a child reciting a biblical verse that serves as a proof-text for the preceding theological discussion about God's patience.
Rav relates that he found a hidden scroll in the house of Rabbi Hiyya containing a teaching by Isi ben Yehuda regarding the thirty-nine prohibited labors of Shabbat.
Rava sees Rav Hamnuna praying at length and rebukes him for prioritizing prayer over Torah study.
A man was heard offering 'achvana' for sale, and it was discovered that he was referring to willow branches, resolving a dispute between Rav and Shmuel.
While sitting before Rabbana Neḥemya, Ravin observes his silk garment and attempts to identify it as the 'kalakh' mentioned in the Mishna, leading to a brief debate with Abaye.
Ravin and Abaye walk through the Valley of Tamrurita and identify certain willow trees as the 'idan' mentioned in the Mishna.
Two elders in Sidon followed different practices regarding Hanukkah lights, one following Beit Shammai and the other Beit Hillel.
Rav Yosef observes his wife lighting Shabbat lamps late and instructs her to light earlier by citing the biblical precedent of the pillars of cloud and fire.
Rav ate dates and threw the pits into an oven on a weekday, leading Rabbi Ḥiyya to warn him that doing so on a Festival would be prohibited.
When Rav arrived in Babylonia, he ate dates on a Festival and threw the pits to animals.
Avin of Tzippori dragged a bench on a marble floor in front of Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Elazar, who then rebuked him by comparing the silence of other sages to his own potential silence.
The head of the synagogue in Batzra dragged a bench before Rabbi Yirmeya, who challenged the legality of his action.
Rabbi Tanḥum is asked a legal question about Shabbat and begins a long homiletical response.
Abaye observes Rava looking toward the west on Shabbat eve to determine the time and questions him based on a baraita regarding the signs of twilight.
Rava instructs his attendant to light the Shabbat lamp as soon as he sees the sun atop the trees, rather than waiting for the stars.

Rav Yosef cites the fact that food was left on the stove for Rav Yehuda and he ate it as evidence for the permissibility of the practice, though Abaye argues this was only due to Rav Yehuda's medical danger.
A legal dilemma is posed to Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba.
Rabbi Yosei travels to Tzippori and finds people leaving water and eggs on the fire, leading him to permit the water but forbid the eggs.
Rav Ḥama bar Ḥanina recounts a time he and Rabbi Judah HaNasi were served and ate many small, well-cooked eggs while being hosted.
Rav Oshaya recounts a time when he and others were standing before Rabbi Hiyya on Shabbat and passed him a kettle of hot water.
The Gemara describes how bathhouse attendants' deceptive practice of heating water on Shabbat led the Sages to prohibit hot water bathing entirely.

Rabbi Zeira observes Rabbi Abbahu floating in a bathhouse on Shabbat but is unsure if he was technically swimming. Rabbi Zeira observes Rabbi Abbahu's modest physical conduct while bathing in the bathhouse.
When Zoroastrian priests threatened to seize Hanukkah lamps, Rav permitted moving the lamps on Shabbat to hide them.
Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Assi visit Rabbi Abba of Haifa, and a candelabrum falls onto their clothing, creating a dilemma about moving it on Shabbat.
Rav Malkiya and Rabbi Yosei the Galilean visit other rabbis and move lamps, causing their hosts to become angry.
Rabbi Romanus reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permitted him to move a coal pan, leading to a confrontation where Rabbi Asi is momentarily silenced by a contradiction.
In the house of Rav Hama, they used to reassemble a collapsible bed on Festivals, leading a sage to question Rava on the legal basis for the practice.
A sage recalls his father, a tanner, telling the family to bring hides to sit on during Shabbat.
Rabbi Hanina ben Akiva once went to a certain place and sat on palm branches that had not been tied together before Shabbat.
A disciple from the Upper Galilee approaches Rabbi Eliezer to clarify traditions he heard regarding distinctions between types of rings and needles.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Yosef reports Rav's lenient ruling on fodder baskets to Shmuel, who responds by questioning Rav's knowledge of Shabbat laws.
Rabbi Zeira travels to Eretz Yisrael and hears Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Yoḥanan, noting that it aligns with Shmuel's (Aryokh's) view in Babylonia.

The Talmud explains that the cow famously associated with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's violation of Shabbat actually belonged to his neighbor, but was attributed to him because he failed to protest her actions.
Rabbi Zeira urges Rabbi Simon to rebuke the members of the Exilarch's household, but Rabbi Simon demurs, claiming they will not listen.
Rav Yosef recounts a dream he had while dozing at a lecture in which a hand from heaven reached out to accept the repentance of Okvan bar Neḥemya.
Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua reports that his sisters do not mind the woven chains in their hair and consequently immerse in the ritual bath without removing them.
The Gemara mentions that Rabbi Akiva made a 'city of gold' ornament for his wife.
When Levi and Rabba bar Avuh permitted the kelila ornament, large numbers of women in their respective cities immediately began wearing them in public.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks his attendant for a sandal and rebukes him for bringing the right one first, implying it makes his foot seem wounded.
Rav Ḥisda reports that because he was meticulous in using large amounts of water for ritual hand-washing, he was rewarded with great prosperity.
Rav Kahana reflects on how he had mastered the entire Talmud by age eighteen but only recently realized the principle that scripture never loses its literal meaning.
Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yosei reports seeing the High Priest's frontplate in Rome and describes its inscription.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Yannai are reported to have walked into public domains with cloths in their ears, prompting disagreement from their peers.
A tanna recites a version of a mishna before Rabbi Yoḥanan, who corrects him and insists on a different reading based on legal logic.
When Rav Huna, Rav, and Rabbi Ḥiyya would leave their respective teachers' homes in a state of intoxication, the teachers would rub oil and salt on them as a remedy.
Rabbi Zeira encounters Rav Yehuda in a particularly good mood and takes the opportunity to ask him a series of questions about the names and nature of various creatures and objects.
Rav Huna questions his son Rabba on why he avoids Rav Hisda's lectures, and Rabba explains that he finds Rav Hisda's focus on anatomy and hygiene to be 'mundane matters.'
Moses encounters God tying crowns to the letters of the Torah and is prompted by God to offer a greeting.
Shmuel recounts how he questioned seafarers to identify the substance 'eshlag' mentioned in the Mishna.
Rav Kahana was standing before Rav and passed a locust over his mouth, leading Rav to tell him to remove it so people wouldn't think he was eating it.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak permits the removal of a corpse to a karmelit in the city of Derokera on Shabbat, leading to a brief legal challenge by Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Rav relates how he found a hidden scroll in the house of Rabbi Hiyya containing a teaching by Isi ben Yehuda regarding the thirty-nine labors.

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira rebukes Rabbi Akiva for identifying the anonymous wood-gatherer as Zelophehad, warning him he will be held accountable for either slandering a righteous man or revealing what the Torah concealed.
Rav Mordekhai travels between Rava, Rav Yosef, and Abaye asking the same legal question, eventually rebuking them all for providing the same answer from the Mishna.
Rabbi Eliezer cites the case of Ben Stada, who smuggled magic spells out of Egypt by scratching them onto his skin.

The Gemara records the specific methods used by Rav Yehuda, Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov, and Rav Sheshet to perform acts of 'anger' (like breaking things or throwing brine) to discipline their households without actually violating prohibitions or causing real damage.
A Boethusian challenges Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi regarding the source for using only kosher skins for phylacteries.
While Bar Liva’ei was standing before Mar Ukva on Shabbat, he observed Mar Ukva applying eye salve in a specific manner, which Mar Ukva then justified based on Shmuel's teaching.
Ulla visits Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda and is presented with hyssop, leading to a discussion on its identification.
Rabbi Yoḥanan corrects his teacher Ḥizkiya by citing Ḥizkiya's own previous ruling, leading Ḥizkiya to praise him as an angel.
Rav Ashi observes Rav Kahana's specific physical practice of holding two loaves but breaking only one, while Rabbi Zeira's habit of breaking a large piece is also noted.
The Roman Emperor asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya for the secret spice that makes Shabbat food smell so good, only to be told it only works for those who observe the day.
A sage would seek out pairs of scholars talking on Shabbat and exhort them to ensure they were properly delighting in the day.
Rabban Gamliel and his companions use a ramp built by a gentile on Shabbat to disembark from their ship, justifying it because the ramp was not built specifically for them.
Rav Kahana visits Rav's house, and Rav instructs his attendants to bring or move a net for Kahana to sit on.
Rav Mari bar Raḥel asks Rava if he may move his felt cushions out of the sun on Shabbat, and Rava provides a permissive ruling.
An anonymous merchant offers 'koranita' for sale and is discovered to be selling thyme, which the Gemara uses to identify the plant.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Ami visits Rav Ḥisda and observes the household moving raw duck meat from the sun to the shade on Shabbat.
The daughter of Rav Hisda immersed in a ritual bath within thirty days of giving birth while her husband was away.
Rav Yosef recalls how students at Rav Huna's academy would cease their studies on days deemed dangerous for bloodletting.
An incident where a circumcision scalpel was forgotten and subsequently brought on Shabbat via roofs and courtyards.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna visit the son of Rav Idi bar Avin, who prepares a calf for them that was slaughtered on its eighth day.
Rav Yosef observes that in Rav Huna's house, canopies were spread in the evening and dismantled by morning, proving the permissibility of these actions on Shabbat.
The Sages enter the vineyard at Yavne and declare that the Torah is destined to be forgotten.
It narrates a specific conflict between Rav's public announcement and Rav Amram Ḥasida's physical enforcement (lashes), involving different actors and a distinct outcome from the subsequent story.
Rav Mesharshiya would pay a gentile child to sow hops for him to avoid legal prohibitions.
The Rabbis report to Rav Ashi that Rav Huna used a piece of garlic as a makeshift plug/filter, and Rav Ashi defends the practice as a permissible form of artifice for a scholar.
The mothers and wives of sages prepare mustard on Shabbat, but their students/sons refuse to eat it, leading to a confrontation about their stringency.
Rav Aha bar Yosef, leaning on his nephew while walking, visits Rav Safra to ask about laundering a shirt on Shabbat and later explains the reasoning to his nephew.
Rav Ḥisda recounts his personal history of abstaining from eating vegetables during both his periods of poverty and wealth to manage his appetite and health.
Rava instructs his servant to roast a duck and feed the remains to a cat on a Festival.
Rav Safra recounts visiting Rabbi Abba and eating a specially prepared chicken that was so rich it would have endangered him had he not drunk wine.
Rav Gaza reports that on one occasion he visited a certain place and prepared a Babylonian kutaḥ dish.
Rav and his students find no room in a certain place, so Rav sits in a carmelit but refuses to sit on felt cushions brought to him.
While Rav Avya was sitting before Rav Yosef, his hand became dislocated, and through the course of their interaction, it was healed.
The Roman emperor asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya why he has not attended the House of Avidan, and the Rabbi responds with a series of metaphors describing the physical decline of old age.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks Rabbi Shimon ben Ḥalafta why he did not visit during the festival, and Shimon explains how the physical toll of old age has made the journey impossible.
While Rav Kahana is reading verses to Rav, Rav sighs upon hearing a verse about old age, leading Rav Kahana to remark on Rav's loss of physical desire.
An apostate challenges Rabbi Abbahu regarding the location of souls and the biblical story of Samuel and the necromancer.
Abaye observes Rabba sliding his son on a donkey on Shabbat and challenges the legality of the act.
Levi reports to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that people in Babylonia knead shatit on Shabbat, causing the Rabbi to cry out in protest.
While it follows the same 'written in the notebook' formula as Passage A, it introduces a new actor (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) and a completely different subject matter (astrological/birth traits).
The Rabbis attended to Rav Zutra, the son of Rav Zeira, and dissolved his vow on Shabbat even though he had time to do so previously.
Ulla visits the Exilarch's house and observes Rabba bar Rav Huna measuring the water in his bathing tub on Shabbat, leading to a discussion on the permissibility of measuring.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi would recite protective verses against evil spirits at night until he fell asleep.
When Rabbi Yonatan asks for the biblical source of the prohibition of a menstruating woman, Rabbi Shimon throws a clod of earth at him in reproach for asking about such an obvious law.
The Gemara cites an incident from the time of King Shapur involving a giant snake that consumed thirteen stables of straw to challenge a Mishnaic ruling about impossible oaths.
Rav Yosef sends a message to Rav Nachman asking him to judge Rav Ulla favorably in a pending trial, leading Rav Nachman to consider how to honor the request without biasing the court.
Rav Nachman navigates the protocol of honoring the wife of a Torah scholar during a trial without intimidating her opponent.
Ameimar seats all witnesses in a trial to honor Rav Yeimar, prompting a legal challenge from Rav Ashi regarding the requirement for witnesses to stand.
The Gemara alludes to the famous incident of Rava's cane, where a debtor hid money inside a hollow staff to technically swear a true oath while deceiving his creditor.
A debtor denies a loan existed, but the creditor's witnesses testify that the loan was made and already repaid, leading Abaye to rule on the debtor's status.
A debtor claims he repaid a loan in front of two witnesses, but the witnesses appear and testify that no such event occurred.
A creditor presents a note, the debtor claims payment, and the creditor's admission of receiving money (even if for a different debt) leads Rav Nachman to rule the note is undermined.
Rav Sheshet encounters Rabba bar Shmuel and asks him to cite any baraitot he knows concerning the laws of a hired worker.
The Sages in Babylonia send a query to Rabbi Elazar in Eretz Yisrael regarding the nature of an oath, and he sends back a ruling.
Rav Yosef bar Minyumi reports that Rav Nahman once acted in a real case by splitting the disputed amount.
A Torah scholar challenges a judge's ruling, promising to bring a letter from Eretz Yisrael to disprove it, to which the judge agrees to yield if the letter is produced.

Rabbi Yehuda recalls his friend Minyamin, an Egyptian convert and student of Rabbi Akiva, who declared his intention to marry his daughter to another Egyptian convert to eventually permit his descendants to enter the congregation.
Miriam prophesies the birth of a savior, and when Moses is born and fills the house with light, her father kisses her in recognition.
Kings who came to fight the family of Jacob changed their minds upon seeing Joseph's crown on Jacob's casket and hung their own crowns there in honor.
When Esau prevents Jacob's burial at the Cave of Machpelah, the deaf Hushim, frustrated by the delay, kills Esau, allowing the burial to proceed.
While the Israelites were busy with loot, Moses sought out Serah daughter of Asher to find Joseph's coffin and miraculously caused it to float to the surface of the Nile.
Rabbi Yehuda recounts an incident where Neḥunya the ditch digger testified that a woman may drink the bitter waters a second time, and the Sages accepted his testimony.
Rabbi Yoḥanan overhears a maiden praying that people should not stumble because of her, from which he derives a lesson on the fear of sin.
Rabbi Yoshiya reports traditions he received from Ze’eira of Jerusalem to the scholars in the South, who accept two of the rulings but reject the third regarding a rebellious elder.
Two students sitting before Rava each report a different biblical verse they heard in their respective dreams.
The angel Gabriel came and taught Joseph seventy languages.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei recounts how he confronted the Samaritans and proved they had forged their Torah by adding specific place names.
Three rabbis located the stones taken from the Jordan River, stood on them, and measured their weight to be forty se’a each.
The spies hide in cedar trees during a Canaanite funeral and overhear the locals comparing them to grasshoppers.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua explains to his disciples that his longevity is due to his lifelong habit of respecting the sanctity of synagogues and the dignity of people.
Passage B describes a distinct behavioral change in Rabbi Abbahu regarding liturgical practice, whereas Passage A describes a distinct realization regarding his character trait of humility.
Rabbi Abbahu declines the headship of the yeshiva in favor of the impoverished Rabbi Abba of Akko.
Abaye boasts that he is as sharp as Ben Azzai, prompting a sage to challenge him with a complex legal problem regarding two corpses found one on top of the other.
Rav Kahana accompanies Rav Shimi bar Ashi to a palm grove and asks him about the origin of the trees there.
The biblical story of Elisha being taunted by youths and the subsequent bear attack.
Elisha travels to Damascus to convince Gehazi to repent, but Gehazi refuses, claiming he learned from Elisha that a public sinner cannot repent.
Rav Huna banned music leading to an economic surplus where goods were cheap but unwanted, until Rav Ḥisda restored it.
Rabba bar Rav Huna made a tambourine for his son, but his father Rav Huna broke it to ensure it wouldn't be confused with a prohibited drum.
Rav Ashi encounters Rav Kahana physically constructing a sukkah with both an expansive handbreadth and a doorway form and questions his stringency.
Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna visit the Exilarch and are lodged by Rav Nahman in a sukkah they would normally consider unfit, yet they remain silent.
While Rav Yosef is citing a teaching to Rav Huna, Rav Huna corrects the attribution, causing Rav Yosef to turn his face away in anger.
Rav Mattana recounts an incident where he brought a doubt regarding ritual fringes to Shmuel, who ruled them permanently unfit.
When Rav Nahman visits Sura, Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna consult him on a ruling, only to be later rebuked by Rav Huna for not having accepted his own identical ruling earlier.
Abaye finds Rav Yosef sleeping in a bridal canopy within a sukka and challenges him for following a minority opinion, leading Rav Yosef to justify his practice based on a variant baraita.
Rabbi Zeira recounts how he married on the eve of Sukkot and combined the wedding celebration with the mitzva of dwelling in the sukkah, resulting in double joy.
The Gemara records two instances where Rav and Rava permitted their students to sleep outside the standard sukka conditions due to physical distress from flies and foul-smelling clay.
The steward of King Agrippas asks Rabbi Eliezer how to fulfill the Sukka requirements given his habit of eating once a day and his two homes.
Rav Huna instructs merchants to have gentiles cut myrtle branches themselves to ensure a legal change of possession.
Rabbi Yehuda begins to cite an incident regarding the four species.
Shmuel confronts myrtle merchants, threatening to publicly rule according to a more lenient opinion if they do not lower their prices.
Rabba instructs the professional lulav-binders of the Exilarch's household to leave a space for the hand to touch the lulav directly.
Aivu witnesses a man bringing a willow to Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok, who performs the ritual by shaking it without reciting a blessing.
A man comes to Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok to report that his workers are hoeing his olive groves during the Sabbatical year.
Rav Kahana relates a personal incident where he traveled on a Friday and was unable to find any food upon arrival.
Rav Mari and Mar Zutra report on the physical practices of Rava, Rav Pappi, and the school of Rav Ashi regarding the donning of phylacteries.
Two heretics named Sason and Simḥa debate their relative importance using biblical verses, ending in Simḥa's witty put-down.
A heretic named Sason mocks Rabbi Abbahu regarding the afterlife, but the Rabbi uses a grammatical nuance to prove the heretic will be the one serving.
Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok describes how young priests would descend into a gap by the altar every seventy years to collect congealed wine residue.
The Gemara describes the immense physical strength of the son of Marta daughter of Baitos, who could carry two heavy bull thighs while walking slowly.
Hillel the Elder sees a floating skull and uses it as a lesson on the principle of measure for measure.
Levi performs a difficult prostration before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and is injured, becoming lame.
Shmuel instructs messengers to go to Rav (calling him Abba) and challenge his ruling on the transition of mentioning rain during the Festival.
Rabbi Ami alludes to the famous legend of the marten and the pit, where a young man rescues a girl and they swear an oath of fidelity witnessed by the marten and the pit.
During a simultaneous famine and plague in the days of Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani, the Sages decided they could only pray for the relief of one affliction at a time and chose the plague.
When a decree forbade fasting in the days of Rabbi Zeira, he instructed the community to commit to the fast immediately so it would be credited to them, even if they could only perform it later.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yoḥanan would claim to be fasting until he reached his home as a pretext to leave the House of the Nasi.
When the Sages told the blind Rav Sheshet that other rabbis were wearing shoes on a fast day, he became angry and sarcastically suggested they might as well have eaten too.
Rav Yehuda appointed his son Rav Yitzḥak to expound publicly, and Rav Yitzḥak subsequently taught the laws of the Aneinu prayer.
The people of Nineveh inquired of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi regarding the protocol for fasting for rain during the summer months in their specific climate.
The general Nicanor would daily wave his hand toward Jerusalem and threaten to conquer it.
Rav and Shmuel, who avoided a dilapidated wall for thirteen years, finally walk past it when the meritorious Rav Adda bar Ahava is with them.
When a plague skips Rav's neighborhood, a dream reveals it is due to the merit of a man who lends tools for burials rather than Rav's own merit.
A fire in Drokart avoids Rav Huna's neighborhood, and a dream reveals this was due to the merit of a woman who shared her oven.
Rava is distressed that he receives fewer heavenly greetings than Abaye, but is comforted by the fact that his merit protects his city.
Rabba bar bar Hana describes the immense height of Keren Ophel by noting that an Arab on a camel seen from the top looked like a tiny worm.
Hanan HaNehba would be approached by children during droughts to pray for rain because of his humility.
Passage B is a complete narrative about Rabbi Yona's humble method of praying for rain, distinct from the narrative in Passage A regarding his son Rabbi Mani's persecution by the house of the Nasi.
Two students ask Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elyashiv to pray for their wisdom, but he tells them he no longer has that power.
