Rabbi Yehuda Nesia decrees a fast for rain that fails, leading him to lament his generation's spiritual standing compared to the prophet Samuel.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish are informed of a fast too late to accept it properly, but decide to observe it regardless.
When Rabbi's fast fails to bring rain, Ilfa leads the prayer and the wind and rain respond immediately to his words.
Rav encounters a prayer leader whose prayer brings rain because of his selfless devotion to teaching the children of the poor.
Rav Nahman's self-deprecating anguish over his failed prayer for rain causes Heaven to respond with rain.
Rabba discusses why his generation's prayers are not answered compared to Rav Yehuda's generation, despite their superior Torah study.
Rav Mari witnesses angels turning sand into flour during the famine but warns the people it is a miracle that will not last.
Rabba describes a vision of the angel Ridya, who looks like a calf and commands the celestial and subterranean waters to provide rain.
When rain falls early during a fast decreed by Shmuel HaKatan, he tells a parable to explain that God granted the rain quickly only to stop hearing their voices.
On another occasion, rain falls after sunset following a fast, and Shmuel HaKatan again rebukes the people's assumption that this indicates their merit.

In Lod, after a fast was decreed and rain fell, the people ate and drank before reciting Hallel. Rav Pappa arrived at a synagogue, decreed a fast, and when rain fell before noon, he instructed the people to recite Hallel.
Abraham expresses concern to God about Israel's survival after the Temple's destruction, leading God to establish the reading of the sacrificial order as a means of atonement.
Shimon HaTzaddik went out to meet Alexander the Great while wearing his priestly vestments.
Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok recounts an incident where three hundred priests were required to move the massive golden vine of the Temple.
Rabbi Elazar ben Diglai recounts how his father's goats in Mikhvar would sneeze from the scent of the incense being prepared in the Jerusalem Temple.
Rav Dimi arrives in Eretz Yisrael, hears Rav Yirmeya teaching a tradition that resolves a difficulty held by Rav Yosef in Babylonia, and expresses a desire to send him a letter.

Rav Dimi's intent to write a legal letter to Rav Yosef leads to a discussion on the prohibition of writing the Oral Law, resolved by the precedent of Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish using written Aggada books.
Rabbi Pappeyas testifies about a specific incident where he owned a cow whose offspring was sacrificed as a peace offering on a festival following the mother's sacrifice on Passover.
Ben Antigonus brought firstborn animals from Babylonia to the Temple, but the authorities refused to accept them for sacrifice.
Rabbi Abbahu would change his practice regarding moving a lamp on Shabbat depending on whether he was in the locale of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi or Rabbi Yoḥanan.
An incident is cited where Rabban Gamliel performed levirate marriage with the rival wife of his own daughter after his brother Abba died.
Rabbi Akiva collected an etrog on the first of Shevat and tithed it twice to satisfy the opinions of both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.

When asked to rule on a sensitive matter of lineage, Rabbi Yehoshua declines to give a theoretical ruling and instead testifies about two prominent Jerusalem families who lived according to the lenient view.
While Rav Hamnuna is studying before Ulla, Ulla praises his greatness but then insults his city's lineage, causing Hamnuna to become embarrassed.
Ameimar permits a relationship, but Rav Hillel challenges him by testifying that he saw a written list of prohibitions by Mar son of Rabbana that included more cases.
Bar Shatya, a man of fluctuating sanity, sold property, leading to conflicting witness testimony and a judicial ruling by Rav Ashi.

Rabbi Ḥiyya and Bar Kappara engage in a heated dispute over Temple laws, where both jump and swear oaths regarding their conflicting traditions, leading Rabbi Ḥiyya to attempt to prove his point through logical deduction.
An incident occurred where a man betrothed a woman within three months of her divorce and fled, and Rafram ruled that his flight was sufficient punishment.
Rabbi Yannai expels Rabbi Hanina Kara from the study hall for reciting a legal ruling that Yannai considers incorrect.
After being silenced by Rav Hamnuna's legal objection, Rava waits for him to leave the study hall before articulating a defense based on the rulings of Rabbi Elazar.
A man approaches Rabbi Yosei to ask if he may perform halitza within three months of a death, and Rabbi Yosei uses a biblical verse to deny the request.
Rabbi Elazar misses a day at the study hall and asks Rabbi Asi to recap the legal rulings taught in his absence.
While leaning on his attendant Rabbi Nahum during a walk, Rabbi Abbahu is questioned on various principles of Mishnaic authority.
Rava caused a man to lose his prepared betrothal feast by ruling that the betrothal was prohibited on the ninetieth day.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin visits a town and rules that the child of an unmarried woman and a slave is fit for marriage.
Rava validates the lineage of Rav Mari bar Raḥel and appoints him to a position of authority in Babylonia.
The slave of Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Ami immerses a gentile woman for marriage, and Rav Yosef later validates her status based on her subsequent habitual immersions.
Rabbis defend the status of individuals whose lineage was questioned by pointing out that their habitual ritual immersions functioned as valid conversions.
Rabbi Shimon ben Azzai recounts finding a genealogical scroll in Jerusalem that recorded specific illicit lineages.
Rav Sheshet flogged a man who was caught passing by the entrance of his father-in-law's house.

The Gemara explains that during the war with Midian, the Israelites identified which girls were of age by passing them before the High Priest's frontplate, which caused a physical reaction in their faces.
The Gemara describes a physical test involving wine barrels used to determine the virginity of the women of Jabesh-gilead.
Rav Sheshet explains his refusal to remarry by revealing he became impotent due to the extreme length of Rav Huna's lectures.
Rabbi Yosei meets Elijah the prophet and asks how a woman helps a man, to which Elijah explains her role in processing raw materials into food and clothing.
Rav enters a field, sees the crops waving in the wind, and remarks that business is more profitable than farming.
The Sages confront Ben Azzai for preaching about procreation while remaining single, and he responds that his soul is in love with the Torah.
The Sages urge Rabbi Abba bar Zavda to remarry to have children, but he refuses, claiming his lack of merit from his first marriage would persist.
Several rabbis became impotent or ill due to the length of Rav Huna's lectures and the physical strain of holding back their bodily needs.
When Rabbi Abbahu (or Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba) cited a ruling in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi physically turned their faces away in protest.
A woman seeking a divorce for infertility was initially rejected by Rabbi Ami, but after she argued she needed children to support her in old age, he compelled the husband to pay.
Shmuel instructs Rav Hana of Baghdad to gather ten men so that he can publicly declare a specific legal ruling regarding a fetus's ability to acquire property.

The Sages challenge Rabbi Yehuda's safety concerns by citing the historical precedent of many men in the time of Ben Koziva who underwent circumcision for drawn foreskins and successfully fathered children.
Rabbi Yoḥanan is silenced by Rabbi Elazar's legal objection and later praises him to Reish Lakish as teaching like Moses.
An uncircumcised priest sprinkled the purification waters and the Sages validated the act.
Minyamin, an Egyptian convert and peer of Rabbi Yehuda, describes his conversion and subsequent marriage to a fellow first-generation convert.
After being silenced by a difficult question, Rav Dimi is helped by Abaye and praises Abaye's sharp mind.
Students ask Rabbi Eliezer about the status of a tenth-generation mamzer, and he responds by suggesting that mamzerim do not even survive to the third generation.
Rabbi Ami publicly identifies a neighbor as a mamzer, causing the man to weep until the Rabbi explains that the public knowledge will actually allow him to live longer.

In the time of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the Sages attempted to permit the Gibeonites to marry into the congregation, but Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi blocked the move by arguing that they could not nullify the portion of the Gibeonites dedicated to the Altar.
Rava Tosfa’a ruled that a child born twelve months after the father's departure was legitimate, accepting the possibility of a delayed pregnancy.
Rabba bar Avuh told the Sages to check if Rav Naḥman's body produced steam in the bath to determine if he was fit to marry his daughter.
Rabbi Ami cites an incident involving a tumtum from Biri who underwent surgery to reveal his male anatomy and subsequently fathered seven children.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalls how, when he went to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua, the other students swarmed around him aggressively like chickens.
When people brought cases of delayed maturity to Rava, he would instruct them to change the person's weight to see if physical signs of puberty would appear.
When the sons of Yudan the maidservant were freed, Rav Aha bar Yaakov permitted them to marry each other's wives, leading to a dispute with Rava.
Rabbi Yehuda recalls a time they were sitting before Rabbi Tarfon and a woman came to perform halitza.
It records a specific historical action taken by Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, which is distinct from the actors in Passage A, though it borders on a bare report of practice.
Rav explains that he only permits certain sandals because he once witnessed his uncle, Rabbi Hiyya, using them for halitza.
A heretic mocks Rabban Gamliel by claiming God performed halitza on Israel, but the Sage retorts that the verse actually implies Israel performed halitza on God, which carries no legal weight.
Rabba bar Ḥiyya performed a ḥalitza ceremony alone at night using a slipper, prompting Shmuel to sarcastically remark on his reliance on individual opinions.
A couple performs halitza while in prison, and Rabbi Akiva subsequently rules the act valid.
It describes a specific ritual practice of Mar Zutra that is challenged by Mar bar Idi and ultimately upheld by the Gemara, constituting a distinct narrative unit with a conflict and resolution.
Rabbi Yehuda recounts a time when a woman came for halitza and Rabbi Tarfon instructed the students to participate in the recitation.
Beit Hillel cites a historical precedent where the wife of Pishon the camel driver successfully performed refusal in her husband's absence.
The daughters-in-law of Abdan rebelled against their husbands, and after an investigation by Sages, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi declared their behavior a valid act of refusal.
Rav Nahman encounters Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rav Hana debating in the Pumbedita market and joins their discussion regarding the levirate status of a minor and a deaf-mute.
A yavam and yevama who both admit they did not have intercourse come before Rava, who instructs his students to arrange a chalitza for them.
Rav Malkiyyu arranged a marriage for his deaf-mute neighbor and proactively secured a high-value marriage contract for the wife from the husband's property.
A woman comes before Rava to testify that her husband died in a famine, leading Rava to change his legal position and equate famine with war regarding the reliability of a wife's testimony.
A man deposits sesame plants with a friend, but when he asks for them back, the friend claims they have already been returned, leading to a dispute over identifying marks.
A bill of divorce belonging to Androlinai is found in Neharde’a, and Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sends it to be verified.
Rava bar Avuh collects money based on two promissory notes found in Meḥoza with palindromic names.
A bill of divorce is found in Sura belonging to Anan bar Ḥiyya, prompting the Sages to search the region and discover another man with the same name, leading to a debate on the document's validity.
A woman comes to Rabbi Yehuda's court to testify her husband died, and the court attendants coach her on how to perform mourning rituals so the court will accept her testimony.
Rabba bar bar Hanna witnesses an Arab cut open a camel with a sword, causing it to die instantly.
Rabbi Meir cites an incident where a man fell into a deep cistern and survived for three days before emerging.
Despite his father's merit in providing water to the public, the son of Neḥunya the well digger dies of thirst.
Yoḥanan the High Priest sent emissaries to investigate tithing practices and, upon finding neglect, instituted the decree of demai.
Rav Ḥaviva bar Surmakei travels to Eretz Yisrael and presents a legal objection to a Sage, who rebukes him for his arrogance in questioning Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rav's students, Rav Kahana and Rav Asi, challenge his prediction that Persia will fall to Rome on the grounds of justice, but Rav maintains it is a divine decree.
Rav Yehuda physically demonstrates the motion of the priestly sprinkling (matzlif) by mimicking the action of a person using a whip.
Marta bat Baitos brought a large sum of money to King Yannai to secure the appointment of Yehoshua ben Gamla as High Priest.
Whenever Rav or Rav Nachman would visit certain cities, they would publicly announce their desire for a woman to marry them for the duration of their stay.
Elijah the Prophet appears to Rav Yehuda to explain that the Messiah has not come because even on Yom Kippur, people are engaging in sin.
The Sages prayed for mercy to abolish the sound made by the soul as it departs from the body, and their prayer was granted.
After Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak mocks the idea of King Saul's purity, he receives a terrifying dream that night and immediately begs Saul's remains for forgiveness.
Ben Katin replaced the two spouts of the Temple laver with twelve spigots so that all twelve priests involved in the daily offering could wash their hands and feet at the same time.
During the Sukkot water libation, a priest intentionally poured the water on his feet, leading the gathered people to pelt him with their etrogim.
Rabbi Yishmael ben Piabi's mother made him an expensive tunic which he wore while performing the Temple service.
A prayer leader performs the confession according to Rabbi Meir's minority view, leading Rabba to challenge him and the leader to defend his choice based on a verse.
Queen Helene donated a gold chandelier to the Temple that reflected sunlight to signal the time for the morning Shema.
The Gemara describes the era of Shimon HaTzaddik's priesthood as a time of consistent miracles in the Temple, which declined into inconsistency and scarcity following his death.
An incident is recorded where the High Priest's voice was heard as far away as Jericho when he pronounced the Divine Name.
Individual testimonies are provided regarding the physical effects of the Temple incense reaching as far as Jericho and the surrounding hills.
During a debate between Rabbi Yirmeya and Ravina, Ravya bar Kisi died, leading the sages to use his death as a mnemonic to remember the specific details of the legal dispute.
A reciter of baraitot presents a ruling to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who rejects it and instructs him to remove that teaching from the house of study.
King Josiah, fearing the prophecy of exile, hides the Ark and other sacred vessels to prevent their capture.
Rava observes Abaye bowing to the right at the end of his prayer and corrects him, explaining he should bow to his left first.
A prayer leader recites the Yom Kippur service order before Rava, who corrects him for mixing conflicting legal opinions in his liturgy.
A Sadducee challenges Rabbi Hanina regarding the impurity of the Jewish people.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei recounts seeing the captured Temple curtain in Rome after being granted access for healing the emperor's daughter.
A wise woman asks Rabbi Eliezer about the different punishments for the Golden Calf, and he dismissively tells her that a woman's wisdom is limited to the spindle.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi physically turn their faces away in silent protest when Rabbi Abbahu recites a ruling they disagree with, because they cannot openly contradict him due to his political ties.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports seeing the site of the Israelite camp and measuring its length.
The students of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai ask why the manna fell daily rather than annually, and he explains it through a parable of a king and his son.
Shammai the Elder refused to wash even one hand to feed his children on Yom Kippur until the Sages intervened and decreed he must use both hands for their well-being.
Rav Yitzhak bar bar Hana reports seeing Ze'iri cross water to visit his student Rav Hiyya bar Ashi.
Rav Yehuda and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda were standing by a river when Rami bar Pappa called out from the opposite bank to ask if he could cross the water to join them.
Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Naḥmani testifies that he saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi wearing cork sandals on Yom Kippur and questioned him about the law.
Rabbi Tzadok is given a small amount of food and demonstrates through his physical actions that it does not require the usual rituals of washing, eating in a sukka, or Grace after Meals.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalls an incident where he and his fellow students ate fruit and bread outside of a sukka while studying with Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua.
A man asks Rava if he may kill another person to save his own life after being threatened by a local ruler.
Following their experience with Kidor, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei begin analyzing names and refuse to stay with a man named Bala.
Rabbi Yoḥanan prepares a remedy for himself on Shabbat and justifies his action to Rav Ḥiyya bar Abba.
A brief report of an incident where rescuers found dead bodies in the upper layer of a collapsed building but continued digging and found survivors underneath.
Bar Hamdudei relates how he stood before Shmuel and observed him reciting a very brief confession.
Ulla bar Rav leads the Ne'ila prayer in front of Rava using a specific combination of verses, and Rava praises his choice.

While lying on his stomach in the study hall, Reish Lakish raises a legal difficulty, dismisses Rabbi Elazar's attempt to answer it as beneath a great scholar, and ultimately provides his own resolution.
Rabba initially disputes Rav Naḥman regarding a sin offering's fitness but retracts his opinion and concedes after hearing a logical proof.
An anonymous elder informs Rabbi Yirmeya that Rabbi Yoḥanan originally introduced the laws of disqualified offerings specifically through the case of a court retracting a ruling.
When Rav Asi's face lit up with joy at Rabbi Yoḥanan's legal answer, Rabbi Yoḥanan clarified that he had only provided a superficial response and the difficulty remained.
Reish Lakish forcefully challenges the Elders of the South regarding their rulings on priests and impurity, leading them to clarify their legal reasoning.
When Rabbi Zeira challenges a legal interpretation, Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba rebukes him sharply, calling him an imbecile.

Levi asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi a legal question which the Rabbi praises, leading the Rabbi's son to challenge the praise as redundant until the Rabbi explains the specific pedagogical reason for Levi's dilemma.
Rav Yehuda uses a hand gesture to demonstrate the physical motion of a priest sprinkling blood like one who whips.
Ravin travels from Babylonia to Israel and presents a legal tradition to Rabbi Yirmeya, who insults him and his Babylonian origins in response.
When the exiles returned to Jerusalem, they physically expanded the dimensions of the altar based on a new understanding of its required placement over the libation cavities.
Shmuel instructs Rav Hana of Baghdad to gather ten men so that he can publicly announce a ruling regarding the burning of impure libations.
Rav Hiyya bar Ashi describes his habitual practice of pouring water on Rav's shoes on Shabbat to serve as a legal precedent regarding laundering leather.

Rav Yitzḥak bar Yehuda leaves Rami bar Ḥama's academy for Rav Sheshet's, leading to a confrontation where Rami bar Ḥama unsuccessfully tries to prove his methodology superior through a legal challenge.
Yosef the Priest's wife died on the eve of Passover, and although he did not want to become impure, the Sages forced him to do so to bury her.
Rav Hamnuna tells Rabbi Zeira not to sit down until he provides a resolution to a specific legal dilemma regarding the impurity of a kosher bird carcass.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports seeing a massive day-old reima offspring the size of Mount Tabor.
A tanna recites a baraita before Rav Adda bar Ahava, who challenges its wording, leading the tanna to suggest erasing the text before being told how to correctly interpret it.
